items.title: DeepSeek Proposes Super-Agent Architecture to Automate AI Coding Workflows
items.summary: Chinese AI company DeepSeek on October 31 published a technical proposal for a ‘super-agent’ architecture designed to coordinate multiple artificial intelligence agents with limited human intervention. The proposal, titled ‘Exploring Super-agent Design: Towards a More Autonomous Agent System’, was published by the DeepSeek Harness team on its official WeChat account. The article outlines an approach to reduce the time developers spend managing individual AI coding sessions. DeepSeek estimated that a person could typically oversee three to five active agent sessions simultaneously, making human attention a constraint on deploying multiple AI assistants. The proposed architecture separates coordination from execution. A central agent, called a Router, receives messages and distributes work to independent agents, or Workers, which execute tasks in parallel and report their results. The Router handles user interactions while the Workers perform assigned tasks. The system is also designed to respond to events such as messages and code updates without requiring explicit instructions for every task. DeepSeek described an example in which an agent detects a software bug reported in a group chat, attempts to reproduce and fix it, and submits a proposed code change for human review. In simulated experiments, DeepSeek’s super-agent architecture recorded a 95th-percentile task completion time of 15.7 minutes, compared with 29.5 minutes for a single-session approach using a neutral prompt and a subagent tool. The experiment involved about 300 messages per run, including around 20 work requests, with each configuration tested five times. DeepSeek said the workload was synthetic and coding tasks were simulated using a tool that consumed time. The tests measured scheduling and coordination capabilities, not the system’s ability to write or fix code. The proposal comes as AI developers expand coding assistants. Anthropic’s Claude Code and OpenAI’s Codex are among the tools designed to handle increasingly complex software development tasks. DeepSeek has also published an open-source research prototype, dsh-superagent-prototype, on GitHub under the MIT License. The prototype supports a single GitHub repository and can optionally listen to messages on Feishu, a workplace collaboration platform. The company said the public prototype is not an official product and differs from its internal implementation. Some architectural ideas in the technical article remain future development directions and are not implemented in the released code. DeepSeek also acknowledged security and privacy risks associated with autonomous agents connected to external services, including prompt injection and potential credential exposure. The company described the public code as a research prototype rather than production-ready software.

items.title: Designing a Reliable Influencer Research Workflow: From Campaign Brief to Creator Shortlist
items.summary: Influencer marketing research often starts with a simple question: How do we find the right creators for a campaign? But the actual process is rarely simple. Marketing teams often switch between social media platforms, spreadsheets, creator profiles, analytics tools, and email inboxes. They collect information in different formats, compare creators manually, and frequently repeat the same research for different campaigns. The real challenge isn't just finding influencers. It's building a repeatable workflow that connects campaign requirements with creator discovery, evaluation, and personalized outreach. Here is a practical framework for organizing that process. 1. Start With a Structured Campaign Brief Before searching for creators, define what a successful partnership should look like. A vague brief such as "We need tech influencers" doesn't provide enough information to guide research. Instead, break the campaign into structured requirements: Campaign objective Target audience Relevant content topics Preferred social platforms Target countries and languages Creator profile and content style Budget range Campaign timeline Excluded topics or creator characteristics For software teams building creator research tools, these requirements can be represented as structured data. For example: { "campaign_objective" : "Product awareness" , "target_audience" : { "regions" : [ "United States" ], "interests" : [ "AI" , "Productivity" , "Technology" ] }, "platforms" : [ "YouTube" , "Instagram" , "TikTok" ], "content_topics" : [ "AI tools" , "Software reviews" , "Productivity workflows" ], "creator_preferences" : { "content_style" : "Educational and practical" , "language" : "English" }, "constraints" : { "budget" : null , "timeline" : null } } The values above are illustrative, not universal campaign requirements. The important idea is to turn natural-language requirements into criteria that can be searched, reviewed, and updated. 2. Use Multiple Discovery Methods Relying on one search method can limit the range of creators you discover. A better approach combines several methods. Keyword-based discovery Start with topics, niches, and phrases that describe the campaign. For example: AI productivity tools AI software reviews No-code automation Developer tools Technology tutorials Try variations of the same topic rather than relying on a single keyword. Similar creator discovery If you already know one creator who matches your target audience, use that creator as a starting point. Look for other creators who cover similar subjects, attract comparable audiences, or publish content in a related style. Content-based discovery Don't evaluate a creator based only on their profile description. Review their recent videos, posts, recurring topics, and the way they communicate with their audience. A creator's actual content often provides more useful context than a short biography. 3. Evaluate Creator Fit Beyond Follower Count One of the most common mistakes in influencer research is treating follower count as the main indicator of campaign suitability. A large audience doesn't automatically mean a good partnership. Consider these five dimensions: 1. Content relevance Does the creator regularly publish content related to your product or industry? 2. Audience alignment Does the available audience information match your target market? 3. Engagement context Look beyond a single engagement percentage. Review views, comments, and interactions across multiple recent posts. 4. Content consistency Does the creator publish regularly? Is their content quality relatively consistent? 5. Collaboration readiness Is there publicly available business contact information? Does the creator appear to work with brands? A useful evaluation table might look like this: Criterion What to review Content fit Recent topics and videos Audience fit Available audience signals Engagement Views and interactions Consistency Publishing patterns Contact Public business information These criteria should support human judgment, not replace it with a single automated score. 4. Build an Evidence-Based Shortlist After reviewing creators, organize them into a shortlist. Instead of saving dozens of profiles without context, record why each creator was selected. A useful shortlist should include: Creator name and profile URL Main content niche Relevant content examples Available performance indicators Audience observations Public business contact information, if available Reason for selection Potential collaboration angle Research status You can also organize creators into three groups: High priority: Strong content relevance and audience alignment. Worth reviewing: Potential fit, but additional research is needed. Low priority: Important campaign requirements are not currently met. This makes it easier for marketing teams to discuss candidates and explain their decisions. 5. Personalize Outreach Instead of Sending Generic Messages Finding a suitable creator is only half the process. The next challenge is starting a meaningful conversation. Generic outreach often looks like this: "Hi, we love your content. Would you like to collaborate with us?" It provides very little context. A better message should explain: Why you selected this creator. Which specific content caught your attention. Why the collaboration could be relevant to their audience. What the proposed partnership involves. What the next step would be. For example: "Hi [Creator Name], I recently came across your content about [specific topic] and particularly enjoyed your approach to [specific detail]. We're exploring a potential collaboration around [campaign topic], and I thought it might be relevant to the audience you've built. Would you be open to discussing a possible partnership? Best, [Your Name]" The key is relevance. A personalized message demonstrates that the brand has actually researched the creator rather than simply collecting their email address. 6. Use AI to Reduce Repetitive Research AI can make creator research more efficient, especially when teams need to process large amounts of information. Some useful applications include: Extracting campaign requirements from natural-language briefs. Expanding keyword ideas for creator discovery. Summarizing publicly available creator profiles and content. Organizing research notes into structured fields. Drafting personalized outreach based on verified context. However, AI-generated insights should be treated as research assistance rather than unquestionable facts. Always verify important information, especially audience data, business contacts, and campaign suitability. Different social platforms also expose different data, so a consistent evaluation process should account for those differences. Human review remains important before contacting creators or making campaign decisions. 7. Measure the Research Workflow A creator research process should be evaluated by more than the number of profiles collected. Consider tracking the following stages: Stage Metric Discovery Creators discovered Evaluation Profiles reviewed Shortlisting Qualified candidates Outreach Messages prepared and sent Response Creator replies Qualification Relevant partnership opportunities These metrics help identify bottlenecks. For example, if a team discovers many creators but only a small number meet campaign requirements, the search criteria may need improvement. If many suitable creators are shortlisted but few respond, the outreach approach may need attention. The goal is to improve the entire workflow, not simply increase the size of the database. Final Thoughts Effective influencer research is a process, not a one-time search. A structured campaign brief, multiple discovery methods, evidence-based evaluation, organized shortlists, and personalized outreach can make the process more consistent and manageable. AI can help reduce repetitive work, but the quality of the final decisions still depends on clear requirements and thoughtful human review. The most useful workflow is one that connects every stage: Understand the brief → Discover → Evaluate → Organize → Outreach. items.summary_html:
Influencer marketing research often starts with a simple question:

How do we find the right creators for a campaign?

But the actual process is rarely simple.

Marketing teams often switch between social media platforms, spreadsheets, creator profiles, analytics tools, and email inboxes. They collect information in different formats, compare creators manually, and frequently repeat the same research for different campaigns.

The real challenge isn't just finding influencers. It's building a repeatable workflow that connects campaign requirements with creator discovery, evaluation, and personalized outreach.

Here is a practical framework for organizing that process.

1. Start With a Structured Campaign Brief

Before searching for creators, define what a successful partnership should look like.

A vague brief such as "We need tech influencers" doesn't provide enough information to guide research.

Instead, break the campaign into structured requirements:

  • Campaign objective
  • Target audience
  • Relevant content topics
  • Preferred social platforms
  • Target countries and languages
  • Creator profile and content style
  • Budget range
  • Campaign timeline
  • Excluded topics or creator characteristics

For software teams building creator research tools, these requirements can be represented as structured data.

For example:

{
  "campaign_objective": "Product awareness",
  "target_audience": {
    "regions": ["United States"],
    "interests": ["AI", "Productivity", "Technology"]
  },
  "platforms": [
    "YouTube",
    "Instagram",
    "TikTok"
  ],
  "content_topics": [
    "AI tools",
    "Software reviews",
    "Productivity workflows"
  ],
  "creator_preferences": {
    "content_style": "Educational and practical",
    "language": "English"
  },
  "constraints": {
    "budget": null,
    "timeline": null
  }
}

The values above are illustrative, not universal campaign requirements.

The important idea is to turn natural-language requirements into criteria that can be searched, reviewed, and updated.

2. Use Multiple Discovery Methods

Relying on one search method can limit the range of creators you discover.

A better approach combines several methods.

Keyword-based discovery

Start with topics, niches, and phrases that describe the campaign.

For example:

  • AI productivity tools
  • AI software reviews
  • No-code automation
  • Developer tools
  • Technology tutorials

Try variations of the same topic rather than relying on a single keyword.

Similar creator discovery

If you already know one creator who matches your target audience, use that creator as a starting point.

Look for other creators who cover similar subjects, attract comparable audiences, or publish content in a related style.

Content-based discovery

Don't evaluate a creator based only on their profile description.

Review their recent videos, posts, recurring topics, and the way they communicate with their audience.

A creator's actual content often provides more useful context than a short biography.

3. Evaluate Creator Fit Beyond Follower Count

One of the most common mistakes in influencer research is treating follower count as the main indicator of campaign suitability.

A large audience doesn't automatically mean a good partnership.

Consider these five dimensions:

1. Content relevance

Does the creator regularly publish content related to your product or industry?

2. Audience alignment

Does the available audience information match your target market?

3. Engagement context

Look beyond a single engagement percentage. Review views, comments, and interactions across multiple recent posts.

4. Content consistency

Does the creator publish regularly? Is their content quality relatively consistent?

5. Collaboration readiness

Is there publicly available business contact information? Does the creator appear to work with brands?

A useful evaluation table might look like this:

Criterion What to review Content fit Recent topics and videos Audience fit Available audience signals Engagement Views and interactions Consistency Publishing patterns Contact Public business information

These criteria should support human judgment, not replace it with a single automated score.

4. Build an Evidence-Based Shortlist

After reviewing creators, organize them into a shortlist.

Instead of saving dozens of profiles without context, record why each creator was selected.

A useful shortlist should include:

  • Creator name and profile URL
  • Main content niche
  • Relevant content examples
  • Available performance indicators
  • Audience observations
  • Public business contact information, if available
  • Reason for selection
  • Potential collaboration angle
  • Research status

You can also organize creators into three groups:

High priority: Strong content relevance and audience alignment.

Worth reviewing: Potential fit, but additional research is needed.

Low priority: Important campaign requirements are not currently met.

This makes it easier for marketing teams to discuss candidates and explain their decisions.

5. Personalize Outreach Instead of Sending Generic Messages

Finding a suitable creator is only half the process.

The next challenge is starting a meaningful conversation.

Generic outreach often looks like this:

"Hi, we love your content. Would you like to collaborate with us?"

It provides very little context.

A better message should explain:

  1. Why you selected this creator.
  2. Which specific content caught your attention.
  3. Why the collaboration could be relevant to their audience.
  4. What the proposed partnership involves.
  5. What the next step would be.

For example:

"Hi [Creator Name],

I recently came across your content about [specific topic] and particularly enjoyed your approach to [specific detail].

We're exploring a potential collaboration around [campaign topic], and I thought it might be relevant to the audience you've built.

Would you be open to discussing a possible partnership?

Best,
[Your Name]"

The key is relevance.

A personalized message demonstrates that the brand has actually researched the creator rather than simply collecting their email address.

6. Use AI to Reduce Repetitive Research

AI can make creator research more efficient, especially when teams need to process large amounts of information.

Some useful applications include:

  • Extracting campaign requirements from natural-language briefs.
  • Expanding keyword ideas for creator discovery.
  • Summarizing publicly available creator profiles and content.
  • Organizing research notes into structured fields.
  • Drafting personalized outreach based on verified context.

However, AI-generated insights should be treated as research assistance rather than unquestionable facts.

Always verify important information, especially audience data, business contacts, and campaign suitability.

Different social platforms also expose different data, so a consistent evaluation process should account for those differences.

Human review remains important before contacting creators or making campaign decisions.

7. Measure the Research Workflow

A creator research process should be evaluated by more than the number of profiles collected.

Consider tracking the following stages:

Stage Metric Discovery Creators discovered Evaluation Profiles reviewed Shortlisting Qualified candidates Outreach Messages prepared and sent Response Creator replies Qualification Relevant partnership opportunities

These metrics help identify bottlenecks.

For example, if a team discovers many creators but only a small number meet campaign requirements, the search criteria may need improvement.

If many suitable creators are shortlisted but few respond, the outreach approach may need attention.

The goal is to improve the entire workflow, not simply increase the size of the database.

Final Thoughts

Effective influencer research is a process, not a one-time search.

A structured campaign brief, multiple discovery methods, evidence-based evaluation, organized shortlists, and personalized outreach can make the process more consistent and manageable.

AI can help reduce repetitive work, but the quality of the final decisions still depends on clear requirements and thoughtful human review.

The most useful workflow is one that connects every stage:

Understand the brief → Discover → Evaluate → Organize → Outreach.

items.title: Sharing an AI agent: what to keep, what to strip, and what never to trust
items.summary: You built an agent that works. Someone asks for it. What do you actually send them? An AI agent is more than a prompt. In AWFlow (a browser automation tool I build) an agent has a model, instructions, memory, skills, rules and routines, and agents can form teams with a handoff map (the coordination runtime behind teams has its own post). We recently added a marketplace where people can share agents and whole teams as templates . That raises a design question every "share your agent" feature has to answer: what's the reusable part, and what's personal? Get it wrong one way and templates are useless. Get it wrong the other way and people leak their memory, their sites and their credentials. Here's how we drew the line, and the rules we follow on install. Never the person: what it knows about its author, or what it is connected to. What travels and what stays An agent template should carry how the agent works , never what it knows about its author or what it's connected to on the author's machine . Drag the line to compare what travels. Here's the full split: Kept (the setup) Stripped (personal or device-specific) Name, handle, role, avatar, greeting, starter prompts Memory and chat history Instructions Knowledge-base contents (the collection references are emptied) Skills it uses (browser, web search, on-device AI…) Credentials and the author's MCP servers Rule preset and generic per-action rules Per-site rules and the author's allow/block site lists Portable routines (schedule, page triggers…) Routines tied to a local workflow or a recording Team: members, roles, way of working, handoff map IDs of the author's own workflows On-device model choice Cloud model choice (it names the author's provider) A few of these deserve a word. Models: on-device travels, cloud doesn't If the author picked an in-browser model, the template keeps it: anyone can download the same model. If they picked a cloud model, the template says "inherit" and the installer's own default applies. A cloud pick names the author's provider and account setup, which the installer may not have. On install, your own default applies. Rules: keep the intent, drop the specifics The agent's rule preset and its generic per-action rules ("ask before submitting forms") are the safety intent, so they travel. Rules tied to specific sites, and the author's allow/block site lists, are personal browsing context, so they're dropped. Peel them apart: the intent travels, the specifics stay home. Dependencies become "needs", not secrets If an agent uses one of the author's workflows as a skill, or an MCP server, the template can't include those. Instead it records what's needed : the workflow's name , the MCP server's host . You get a plain note. After installing, the user sees “Add these to finish setting it up: …”. The agent depends on the author's things A workflow that lives on the author's device, an MCP server they connected. Neither can travel. Export records the need The template keeps the workflow's name and the server's host, so the installer knows what is missing. Install creates the agent The new agent starts without those tools, rather than pretending to have them. You get a plain note After installing, the user sees "Add these to finish setting it up: …" . That's much better than an agent that silently has fewer tools than its description promises. Routines: only the portable ones A routine triggered by a schedule or a page event travels. A routine that depends on a local workflow or a recorded sequence can't work on someone else's machine, so it's left out rather than shipped broken. On install: never trust the file A template is just data, and data from strangers is untrusted. The rule: treat the file as untrusted input. Install follows a few rules: Same guardrails: "ask" asks, locked categories always ask. The re-mapping is worth seeing, because it's where a careless importer leaks or overwrites things. The built-in assistant is reused, not duplicated. The marketplace on top The marketplace adds the social layer. Listings are reviewed by a moderator before they go live, and anyone can browse agent and team templates in Marketplace › Agents & teams without signing in. Installing is one click, plus a single confirmation when the template's agents can act in your browser or run on their own. The install is counted on the server (once per signed-in person), but the agents themselves are created locally on your device. One honest limit: stripping protects your state and your connections, not your words. Instructions are shared as written. The marketplace checks a template again when it is submitted and refuses anything that looks like a key or personal data, but read your instructions before you share. The templates page in the docs lists everything that is and isn't shared. If you're building "share your agent" in your own product, this is the short list: Untrusted on install: fresh IDs, remapped references, same guardrails. AWFlow is free and runs in your browser. Interactive version with animations: https://awflow.io/blog/sharing-an-ai-agent-what-to-strip Try it Agentic Workflow (AWFlow) runs in your browser, on the model you choose, free and with no account needed to start. Install it from the Chrome Web Store here .

items.title: Beyond the AI Demo: Five Product Engineering Companies and What Developers Should Evaluate
items.summary: An AI demo can generate answers, process a document, or complete a workflow. Production introduces harder questions: what happens when the provider times out, a deployment changes output quality, or another team inherits the code? For developers evaluating an external engineering partner, these questions matter more than the speed of the first demonstration. This article examines themes from GeekyAnts’ discussion of AI-powered product engineering , then considers five companies through the lens of engineering responsibilities. The shortlist is not a verified performance ranking. What should survive beyond the prototype? The source article emphasizes modular architecture, model portability, continuous testing, human review, and ownership after launch. It also describes AntFlow AI as a workflow involving agreed specifications, agent-generated implementation, separate verification, and human approval. These are useful evaluation themes, but a provider’s description is only the starting point. The meaningful evidence lies in its implementation artifacts and the experience of the proposed delivery team. A technical assessment should connect each claim to something observable: Provider claim Evidence to request Modular architecture Component boundaries and a walkthrough of a recent change Model portability A demonstrated provider change and its evaluation results Human oversight Review ownership and release approval criteria Production readiness Monitoring, incident procedures, and recovery exercises Long-term ownership Runbooks, repository access, and handover expectations This turns a broad capabilities discussion into a review that engineers can challenge. Which five companies belong in the comparison? GeekyAnts GeekyAnts describes an approach combining product engineering with AI-assisted delivery. Its article places responsibility for architecture, code approval, and deployment decisions with engineers, while using AI for parts of implementation. The relevant assessment is whether those controls operate consistently on the proposed engagement. A sample pull request, verification report, and release checklist would be more informative than a general presentation about development speed. IBM IBM’s application modernization services combine cloud engineering with AI-assisted approaches to existing software estates. Its published offering discusses deterministic code analysis alongside generative and agentic AI. For teams extending established applications, the evaluation should focus on how the proposed team identifies dependencies and validates changed behavior. Buyers should also distinguish reusable delivery tooling from project-specific engineering work. Accenture Accenture’s AI Refinery work includes the Distiller agentic framework and SDKs intended to support development and deployment of enterprise AI solutions. Developers assessing this approach should examine the boundary between framework capabilities and application responsibilities. Useful questions concern deployment ownership, debugging access, portability, and how much custom code remains maintainable by the client’s team. Deloitte Deloitte’s engineering services cover AI application development, data platforms, software platform engineering, and ML/LLM operations. That breadth makes team composition an important evaluation point. A proposal should identify who owns application code, data pipelines, evaluation, and production operations, including how those responsibilities connect when an incident crosses several layers. TCS TCS’ Software Product Innovation Services include AI-led engineering, digital platform development, and product transformation. For a product with an established roadmap, the assessment should examine how modernization and feature delivery coexist. The proposed team should explain its approach to regression testing, release ownership, and preserving product knowledge as contributors change. How can developers test the claims fairly? A bounded technical exercise can make comparisons more useful. For example, each shortlisted team could assess the same document-processing workflow and explain how it would handle an unavailable model provider, an unreadable input, and an output that requires human review. The requested deliverables could include: A component diagram with external dependencies. Explicit success and failure criteria. A small evaluation dataset with expected outcomes. A release and recovery plan. A breakdown of recurring operating costs. The exercise should reflect the intended project. It should also reveal assumptions: what requires further discovery, which behavior remains uncertain, and where human intervention is necessary. What should determine the final decision? The strongest evidence is a delivery team that can explain its engineering choices and their consequences. A polished demo provides limited information about maintainability, incident response, or the cost of operating the product. Likewise, a recognizable company name does not establish the capabilities of the people assigned to a particular engagement. A useful selection process therefore compares named teams, inspectable work, and clearly assigned responsibilities. The practical goal is a product that the client can operate, change, and understand after its first release.
items.summary_html:
An AI demo can generate answers, process a document, or complete a workflow. Production introduces harder questions: what happens when the provider times out, a deployment changes output quality, or another team inherits the code?

For developers evaluating an external engineering partner, these questions matter more than the speed of the first demonstration.

This article examines themes from GeekyAnts’ discussion of AI-powered product engineering, then considers five companies through the lens of engineering responsibilities. The shortlist is not a verified performance ranking.

What should survive beyond the prototype?

The source article emphasizes modular architecture, model portability, continuous testing, human review, and ownership after launch. It also describes AntFlow AI as a workflow involving agreed specifications, agent-generated implementation, separate verification, and human approval.

These are useful evaluation themes, but a provider’s description is only the starting point. The meaningful evidence lies in its implementation artifacts and the experience of the proposed delivery team.

A technical assessment should connect each claim to something observable:

Provider claim Evidence to request Modular architecture Component boundaries and a walkthrough of a recent change Model portability A demonstrated provider change and its evaluation results Human oversight Review ownership and release approval criteria Production readiness Monitoring, incident procedures, and recovery exercises Long-term ownership Runbooks, repository access, and handover expectations

This turns a broad capabilities discussion into a review that engineers can challenge.

Which five companies belong in the comparison? GeekyAnts

GeekyAnts describes an approach combining product engineering with AI-assisted delivery. Its article places responsibility for architecture, code approval, and deployment decisions with engineers, while using AI for parts of implementation.

The relevant assessment is whether those controls operate consistently on the proposed engagement. A sample pull request, verification report, and release checklist would be more informative than a general presentation about development speed.

IBM

IBM’s application modernization services combine cloud engineering with AI-assisted approaches to existing software estates. Its published offering discusses deterministic code analysis alongside generative and agentic AI.

For teams extending established applications, the evaluation should focus on how the proposed team identifies dependencies and validates changed behavior. Buyers should also distinguish reusable delivery tooling from project-specific engineering work.

Accenture

Accenture’s AI Refinery work includes the Distiller agentic framework and SDKs intended to support development and deployment of enterprise AI solutions.

Developers assessing this approach should examine the boundary between framework capabilities and application responsibilities. Useful questions concern deployment ownership, debugging access, portability, and how much custom code remains maintainable by the client’s team.

Deloitte

Deloitte’s engineering services cover AI application development, data platforms, software platform engineering, and ML/LLM operations.

That breadth makes team composition an important evaluation point. A proposal should identify who owns application code, data pipelines, evaluation, and production operations, including how those responsibilities connect when an incident crosses several layers.

TCS

TCS’ Software Product Innovation Services include AI-led engineering, digital platform development, and product transformation.

For a product with an established roadmap, the assessment should examine how modernization and feature delivery coexist. The proposed team should explain its approach to regression testing, release ownership, and preserving product knowledge as contributors change.

How can developers test the claims fairly?

A bounded technical exercise can make comparisons more useful.

For example, each shortlisted team could assess the same document-processing workflow and explain how it would handle an unavailable model provider, an unreadable input, and an output that requires human review.

The requested deliverables could include:

  • A component diagram with external dependencies.
  • Explicit success and failure criteria.
  • A small evaluation dataset with expected outcomes.
  • A release and recovery plan.
  • A breakdown of recurring operating costs.

The exercise should reflect the intended project. It should also reveal assumptions: what requires further discovery, which behavior remains uncertain, and where human intervention is necessary.

What should determine the final decision?

The strongest evidence is a delivery team that can explain its engineering choices and their consequences.

A polished demo provides limited information about maintainability, incident response, or the cost of operating the product. Likewise, a recognizable company name does not establish the capabilities of the people assigned to a particular engagement.

A useful selection process therefore compares named teams, inspectable work, and clearly assigned responsibilities. The practical goal is a product that the client can operate, change, and understand after its first release.

items.title: Your AI Agent Doesn't Read Your 40-Page Security Policy
items.summary: Your company spent three months writing an AI governance policy. Legal reviewed it. Security approved it. Compliance signed off. Engineering received a 40-page PDF. Then someone deployed an AI agent with access to a production database. Here's my question: Which line of that PDF actually stops the agent from executing an unauthorized query? Exactly. This is the uncomfortable reality of enterprise AI governance. We're treating organizational policies as though they automatically translate into technical restrictions. They don't. The Policy Exists. The Permission Still Works. Imagine you're building an AI support agent. It can retrieve customer records and recommend account updates. Your organization has a clear policy: Customer records must not be modified without approval. The system prompt includes the same instruction. But your agent also has access to this tool: update_customer_record ( customer_id , changes ) And the tool itself doesn't enforce approval. Now imagine the agent decides that modifying the record is necessary to resolve a customer issue. If nothing outside the model checks authorization, the operation may execute. Your policy hasn't disappeared. It's just not connected to the execution path. That's not a documentation problem. It's an enforcement problem. We Keep Putting Rules in the Wrong Place There are several ways developers try to control agents. System prompts. Tool descriptions. Workflow instructions. Configuration settings. All of these can be useful. But they serve different purposes. A system prompt can influence what the model decides. A tool description can explain intended usage. A configuration setting can restrict access if the platform actually enforces it. An authorization mechanism can determine whether a proposed action is permitted. These aren't interchangeable. If a model can directly call a sensitive tool without an independent permission check, telling it not to do so is not a sufficient security boundary. The Missing Check A basic enforcement pattern might look like this: def run_tool ( agent , tool , args ): decision = authorize ( agent = agent , tool = tool , args = args ) if decision == " DENY " : return { " status " : " blocked " } if decision == " REVIEW " : return { " status " : " approval_required " } if decision != " ALLOW " : return { " status " : " blocked " } return execute ( tool , args ) Illustrative pseudocode. The model proposes the tool call. The authorization mechanism evaluates it. Only permitted operations execute. The important part isn't the specific code. It's the separation of responsibilities. An AI model shouldn't be the sole authority over its own permissions. What About Approval Workflows? Approval workflows can help, but only if they're genuine execution checkpoints. Consider two designs. Design A The agent sends an email. The system notifies an administrator that a sensitive email was sent. Design B The agent prepares an email. The system detects that approval is required. Execution pauses. An authorized reviewer approves or rejects the action. Only an approved message can be sent. Design A provides visibility. Design B provides enforcement. Both may produce logs. Only one actually prevents the protected action from executing without approval. The Four Questions I'd Ask Before Shipping 1. What happens when authorization fails? Does the system block the action or continue? 2. Can the agent bypass a restriction through another tool? If one tool is blocked, does another provide the same underlying capability? 3. Are approvals bound to the exact proposed action? An approval for one recipient or transaction shouldn't automatically authorize a modified operation. 4. What happens when the policy service is unavailable? For sensitive actions, missing authorization shouldn't silently become permission. These questions are far more useful than simply asking whether the organization has an AI governance policy. The Nuroen Approach At Nuroen AI, we're building enterprise agents around the idea of bounded execution. That includes scope restrictions, confidence checks, policy and human approval gates, execution budgets, and auditability. The goal isn't to eliminate autonomous behavior. It's to ensure that agents can perform useful work without treating every available tool as an unrestricted permission. The Real Lesson Documentation is necessary. Policies are necessary. Security reviews are necessary. But none of them automatically enforce themselves. A policy tells you what should happen. A runtime control determines whether a protected action is allowed to happen. And once AI agents start interacting with production systems, that difference matters. Your governance policy shouldn't live only in a PDF. Its requirements need to exist in the execution path. Question for developers: What's the most common AI agent security mistake you've seen — overpowered tools, missing approval gates, or trusting prompts as permissions? Nuroen AI: https://www.nuroen.com/

Your company spent three months writing an AI governance policy.

Legal reviewed it.

Security approved it.

Compliance signed off.

Engineering received a 40-page PDF.

Then someone deployed an AI agent with access to a production database.

Here's my question:

Which line of that PDF actually stops the agent from executing an unauthorized query?

Exactly.

This is the uncomfortable reality of enterprise AI governance.

We're treating organizational policies as though they automatically translate into technical restrictions.

They don't.

The Policy Exists. The Permission Still Works.

Imagine you're building an AI support agent.

It can retrieve customer records and recommend account updates.

Your organization has a clear policy:

Customer records must not be modified without approval.

The system prompt includes the same instruction.

But your agent also has access to this tool:

update_customer_record(
    customer_id,
    changes
)

And the tool itself doesn't enforce approval.

Now imagine the agent decides that modifying the record is necessary to resolve a customer issue.

If nothing outside the model checks authorization, the operation may execute.

Your policy hasn't disappeared.

It's just not connected to the execution path.

That's not a documentation problem. It's an enforcement problem.

We Keep Putting Rules in the Wrong Place

There are several ways developers try to control agents.

System prompts.

Tool descriptions.

Workflow instructions.

Configuration settings.

All of these can be useful.

But they serve different purposes.

A system prompt can influence what the model decides.

A tool description can explain intended usage.

A configuration setting can restrict access if the platform actually enforces it.

An authorization mechanism can determine whether a proposed action is permitted.

These aren't interchangeable.

If a model can directly call a sensitive tool without an independent permission check, telling it not to do so is not a sufficient security boundary.

The Missing Check

A basic enforcement pattern might look like this:

def run_tool(agent, tool, args):
    decision = authorize(
        agent=agent,
        tool=tool,
        args=args
    )

    if decision == "DENY":
        return {"status": "blocked"}

    if decision == "REVIEW":
        return {"status": "approval_required"}

    if decision != "ALLOW":
        return {"status": "blocked"}

    return execute(tool, args)

Illustrative pseudocode.

The model proposes the tool call.

The authorization mechanism evaluates it.

Only permitted operations execute.

The important part isn't the specific code.

It's the separation of responsibilities.

An AI model shouldn't be the sole authority over its own permissions.

What About Approval Workflows?

Approval workflows can help, but only if they're genuine execution checkpoints.

Consider two designs.

Design A

The agent sends an email.

The system notifies an administrator that a sensitive email was sent.

Design B

The agent prepares an email.

The system detects that approval is required.

Execution pauses.

An authorized reviewer approves or rejects the action.

Only an approved message can be sent.

Design A provides visibility.

Design B provides enforcement.

Both may produce logs.

Only one actually prevents the protected action from executing without approval.

The Four Questions I'd Ask Before Shipping

1. What happens when authorization fails?

Does the system block the action or continue?

2. Can the agent bypass a restriction through another tool?

If one tool is blocked, does another provide the same underlying capability?

3. Are approvals bound to the exact proposed action?

An approval for one recipient or transaction shouldn't automatically authorize a modified operation.

4. What happens when the policy service is unavailable?

For sensitive actions, missing authorization shouldn't silently become permission.

These questions are far more useful than simply asking whether the organization has an AI governance policy.

The Nuroen Approach

At Nuroen AI, we're building enterprise agents around the idea of bounded execution.

That includes scope restrictions, confidence checks, policy and human approval gates, execution budgets, and auditability.

The goal isn't to eliminate autonomous behavior.

It's to ensure that agents can perform useful work without treating every available tool as an unrestricted permission.

The Real Lesson

Documentation is necessary.

Policies are necessary.

Security reviews are necessary.

But none of them automatically enforce themselves.

A policy tells you what should happen.

A runtime control determines whether a protected action is allowed to happen.

And once AI agents start interacting with production systems, that difference matters.

Your governance policy shouldn't live only in a PDF.

Its requirements need to exist in the execution path.

Question for developers: What's the most common AI agent security mistake you've seen — overpowered tools, missing approval gates, or trusting prompts as permissions?

items.title: Guul: connecting a resume builder with the rest of a job search
items.summary: I’m working on Guul , an AI-assisted resume builder and career workspace. This introduction is for people who want to try the workflow and give feedback. A resume is only one part of applying for a job. After tailoring it, there is still the cover letter, the application status, the follow-up, recruiter outreach and interview preparation. Guul brings those tasks into the same workspace. What the workspace includes Resume creation, importing, editing and tailoring to a role. Cover-letter writing. Application tracking and follow-up reminders. Recruiter outreach drafts that the user sends themselves. Mentor review through revocable links. The resume owner chooses which suggestions to apply. Interview practice with Pro access, subject to usage limits. Career-profile publishing. The boundary around ATS checks Guul includes checks for readability and modeled parsing risks. They are simulations. They do not run a resume through an employer’s live applicant-tracking system, and they cannot promise interviews. That distinction matters when evaluating any resume tool. A text extractor recovering words from a PDF is a narrower result than proving how a particular employer will interpret an application. Guul publishes its score methodology and template parse tests so readers can examine the scope rather than relying on a score alone. What is free Editing, previews, TXT downloads, basic checks and several career tools are free. PDF and Word exports require a one-time resume pack or qualifying Pro access. One-time packs provide 30 days of download access without renewal. Optional Pro subscriptions renew until canceled, and AI usage limits apply. Current plans and conditions are on the website. Feedback I would value For developers managing a job search, where does the workflow become fragmented? Would connecting application tracking and mentor review to the resume be useful, or would you prefer those as separate tools? You can explore Guul’s career tools and the resume builder . Disclosure: this post was written by an AI agent. The feature and pricing descriptions were checked against Guul’s public pages.

For developers managing a job search, where does the workflow become fragmented? Would connecting application tracking and mentor review to the resume be useful, or would you prefer those as separate tools?

You can explore Guul’s career tools and the resume builder.

items.title: Northflank Breach Exposes AI API Keys
items.summary: Northflank told every customer to assume that all environment variables stored on its platform had been decrypted and to rotate every key. The October 30 warning followed a threat alert from cloud security company Wiz. Northflank later confirmed that customers had reported unauthorized use of AI API keys supplied to the cloud application hosting platform. Those keys can turn a breach of deployment infrastructure into direct access to metered AI services, with the bill landing on the customer. According to Northflank's published timeline, Wiz alerted the company at 11:43 UTC on October 30. Northflank engineers reviewed the alert one minute later, applied a network policy patch, and deployed additional patches at 12:50 UTC and 13:05 UTC. The company also requested help from Wiz's incident response team. Northflank has not disclosed how the attackers obtained access, how many customers were affected, or whether credentials other than the reported AI API keys were stolen or abused. Its instructions nevertheless set the working scope clearly: rotate user-provided secrets in workloads, secret groups, and global secrets. Customers should also disable public access to add-ons where it is enabled. Environment variables are a common interface between deployment systems and applications. They often contain database passwords, cloud credentials, authentication tokens, and third-party API keys. A platform that can decrypt those variables sits on a dense collection of credentials spanning many customers and services. Once an attacker reaches that layer, each secret can provide another route into a customer's infrastructure or an account capable of generating charges. AI credentials are particularly easy to monetize because the service is consumed through authenticated API requests. Wiz calls the abuse of stolen AI credentials "LLMJacking": attackers use another organization's keys to invoke models, accumulate charges, or resell access. In two cases investigated by Wiz, compromised enterprise credentials made about 2.5 million Amazon Bedrock API calls and generated approximately $100,000 in usage. The Northflank incident was one of at least nine October incidents involving AI development platforms identified by Wiz. The list included Railway, OpenCode, Warp, and Lightning AI. Railway also faced potential exposure of decrypted customer environment variables, OpenCode disclosed exposed AI API keys, and Warp reported exposure of AI agent logs and user telemetry. Wiz has not attributed all nine incidents to the same attackers, although many involved attempts to obtain AI API keys. For Northflank customers, replacing a secret in the platform is only part of the response. The old credential must be revoked or disabled at its issuer. Otherwise, removing it from a workload leaves the captured value usable. Rotation should cover every credential that passed through the affected secret stores, including database passwords and cloud or service tokens, rather than stopping after the visibly abused AI keys. Usage and billing logs at AI providers should be reviewed for unexpected calls. Northflank specifically advised customers to report suspicious usage to both Northflank and the relevant AI provider. Investigation windows should begin before the October 30 disclosure where retained logs allow it, because the alert time establishes when Northflank learned about the incident rather than when access necessarily began. The incident also exposes an operational dependency that credential inventories often obscure. A key may belong to an AI provider, but its effective custody includes the deployment platform that stores and injects it. Rotation procedures therefore need to account for provider-side revocation, platform-side replacement, application rollout, and verification that old instances or jobs no longer carry the previous value. Northflank enabled credential rotation for PostgreSQL, MongoDB, MySQL, and Redis as part of its response. It also enabled audit logs for all customers, including free accounts. Those logs can help identify suspicious platform activity, while provider logs show whether stolen credentials were used elsewhere. Both views are needed when a deployment-layer breach crosses into external services.

items.title: markgate: Mechanically Catch Coding Agent Slip-ups and Enforce Non-Command Tasks
items.summary: I built an OSS tool called markgate that mechanically catches and enforces two kinds of gaps: when a Coding Agent (Claude Code, etc.) accidentally forgets to call a Skill that runs build or tests after implementation and commits anyway, and when AI tasks that can't be reduced to a command — like a /check-docs Skill — can't be enforced through hooks. markgate NOTE: markgate is meant to run inside a git repository. markgate markgate is a CLI tool that acts as an enforcement layer wedged between the Coding Agent and your hooks . By mechanically catching and enforcing the Coding Agent's mistakes and omissions, it addresses the following three failure patterns. Pattern Failure pattern it addresses Solution 1 Catching forgotten calls and avoiding duplicate execution markgate run 2 Enforcing non-command tasks markgate set + markgate verify 3 Scoping multiple tasks + aggregate verify composes in .markgate.yml Below, we'll walk through each pattern in turn. Pattern 1: Catching Forgotten Calls and Avoiding Duplicate Execution ( markgate run ) Suppose you have an implementation skill, and a check skill ( /check ) that runs after it. /check runs verifications against the implemented code. The things you want to guarantee against your implementation will vary by project — tests, typecheck, lint, format, build, documentation consistency, coverage generation, image scans, and so on. However, even if you tell the Coding Agent "run /check after implementing", the Coding Agent can forget and silently skip the step . When that happens, your code gets committed without the checks you wanted to run. So, you set up a pre-commit hook to forcibly run the equivalent of /check . But the Coding Agent doesn't always forget. In fact, forgetting is rare — usually it runs /check just fine. That leads to "the skill already ran it → the hook runs it again", a duplicate execution . If /check is heavy, this slows down what should be a fast Coding Agent development cycle. If it's light you might not notice, but running it frequently still wastes a non-trivial amount of time. Furthermore, if you skip the check after the implementation skill and put all check logic only in the hook, you can't run checks when you're not yet ready to commit. Running a post-edit hook on every file change isn't a great answer either, since the checks then run on every edit and that takes time. Solved with markgate run markgate keeps both the /check skill and the hook in place, and makes it so that the hook fires only when the Coding Agent forgets /check . In other words, when the Coding Agent runs /check properly, the hook is skipped , so duplicate execution doesn't happen. Usage The basic flow is no config file required — just call the command. For example, suppose your /check skill and pre-commit hook from above both run pnpm build . And suppose the pre-commit hook is wired up via Claude Code's PreToolUse hook firing on git commit* . 1. /check skill In the /check skill that runs first, wrap the pnpm build command using markgate run -- . // ... inside the skill definition - pnpm build + markgate run -- pnpm build 2. hook In the pre-commit hook, rewrite pnpm build to markgate run -- pnpm build in the same way. { "hooks": { "PreToolUse": [{ "matcher": "Bash", "if": "Bash(git commit*)", - "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "pnpm build" }] + "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "markgate run -- pnpm build" }] }] } } With just this, you get the behavior where the hook fires only when the Coding Agent forgets /check , running pnpm build . When the Coding Agent runs /check properly, the latter hook is skipped, so duplicate execution doesn't happen. Pattern 2: Enforcing Non-command Tasks ( set + verify ) Up to this point, markgate run has meant writing the target command ( pnpm build , etc.) directly into the hook configuration. In practice, though, there are also tasks that can't be reduced to a command . For example, "is the documentation consistent with src?", "does the PR description match the diff?", "is naming consistent with the existing code?" — these are reviews that need LLM judgment and can't be expressed as a shell command. You want to run this kind of LLM task in the Coding Agent's own session , because you want to leverage the context the Coding Agent has built up (conversation history, open files, past decisions). Technically, you could launch a separate session from a hook via claude -p , but since the context isn't shared , it doesn't act as a continuation of the work so far. As a result, the hook alone can't tell whether the Coding Agent ran an LLM task like /check-docs , which means there's no way to enforce it . Building a Gate with set + verify That's where the gate pattern — combining markgate set and markgate verify — comes in. The check itself stays on the skill side; set records "the moment the check passed" as a marker , and on the hook side, verify acts as a gate that judges whether "the recorded marker matches the current marker". markgate set : records the moment the check passed as a marker markgate verify : exits 0 if the recorded marker matches the current marker, and exits 1 to stop things if they don't match Since the marker records the code state at the time of set , when the code changes afterward the recorded marker and the current marker no longer match , and verify stops things (we'll cover what's inside a marker later). Usage At the end of where the check actually runs (a skill like /check-docs ), call markgate set . On the hook side, just call markgate verify . # At the end of the /check-docs skill definition markgate set // .claude/settings.json (hook side) { "hooks" : { "PreToolUse" : [ { "matcher" : "Bash" , "if" : "Bash(git commit*)" , "hooks" : [ { "type" : "command" , "command" : "markgate verify || { echo 'run /check-docs' >&2; exit 1; }" } ] } ] } } The whole chain of check operations stays defined on the skill side, and the hook just looks at the marker. If the marker is missing or doesn't match the code, the hook blocks with exit 1, and the Coding Agent gets both the error and a hint ( run /check-docs ), so when the gate blocks things, recovery can be left to the Coding Agent and it can loop again . Catching Both "First-time Non-command Triggers" and "Slip-ups" This gate pattern is effective in both of the following cases. First-time non-command trigger : The Coding Agent doesn't even know /check-docs exists and tries to commit. → Since there's no marker, the hook blocks, and after reading the error message ( run /check-docs ), the Coding Agent runs /check-docs for the first time. Slip-up : The Coding Agent runs /check-docs and the marker is set. But later, when the code is edited again and you want to re-check , the Coding Agent forgets to re-run /check-docs . → Since the marker no longer matches the code, the hook blocks and prompts the Coding Agent to re-run. In short, markgate uniformly catches both never-run-before cases and failure to re-run after a slip-up , using the same logic: "does the marker match the current code state?". Pattern 3: Scoping and Aggregate Verify ( .markgate.yml + composes ) So far we've assumed "one skill, one hook", but in practice you often have multiple checks lined up. For example, suppose at pre-commit you want to run light checks ( check : typecheck / lint / build / unit test) plus a heavier check that uses an LLM to verify documentation consistency ( docs ). The problem here is wasted runs . If you bundle them into a single gate, even on a commit that only touches tests, the LLM consistency check runs even though nothing in the documentation-related files changed. That would mean re-running the heavy LLM check every time you change any code, which isn't practical. Giving Each Task Its Own Scope That's where .markgate.yml comes in: give each check its "own scope" (= the set of files specified in include ). Whether a re-run is needed is judged by whether the code change falls within that scope. On top of that, using composes to create an aggregate gate that bundles multiple gates means the hook side can judge "do all the bundled gates match the current code?" with just a single line of verify . Usage Create a .markgate.yml ( markgate init generates a template). # .markgate.yml gates : check : hash : files # only the files specified in include are hashed include : - " src/**" - " tests/**" - " package.json" docs : hash : files include : - " src/**" # changes in src also affect docs, so include in both - " docs/**" - " README.md" pre-commit : composes : [ check , docs ] # aggregate gate: AND of check and docs From the skill side, specify the gate name as an argument and set each gate individually. # At the end of the /check skill definition pnpm typecheck && pnpm lint && pnpm test && markgate set check # At the end of the /check-docs skill definition markgate set docs Then, in the pre-commit hook, verify the pre-commit aggregate gate in a single line. When it doesn't match, markgate status pre-commit shows "which gate doesn't match", and the Coding Agent reads that and re-loops the corresponding skill. // .claude/settings.json { "hooks" : { "PreToolUse" : [ { "matcher" : "Bash" , "if" : "Bash(git commit*)" , "hooks" : [ { "type" : "command" , "command" : "markgate verify pre-commit || { markgate status pre-commit >&2; exit 1; }" } ] } ] } } The key point is that only the checks needed for the edited scope get re-run . Each gate's marker only hashes the files in its own include , so on a commit that only touches one side's scope, the other gate's marker stays the same as when it was set and still matches, meaning no re-run is needed. For example, a commit that only modifies tests re-runs only the light checks; a commit that only touches files outside any include (CI config, etc.) skips both. Edited files check docs Checks that need to re-run tests/** only stale fresh light checks only docs/** / README.md only fresh stale heavy check only src/** stale stale both None of the above (CI config, editor config, etc.) fresh fresh none (commit passes) Note that the pre-commit aggregate gate in this example is designed without a command of its own; it just performs the AND judgment — fresh if all bundled gates are fresh, stale if any one is stale. This shape — without its own command — can't be written with markgate run (which wraps a single command); only the gate pattern ( set + verify ) can express it. Other Use Case Examples Beyond the basic usage above, markgate has various advanced patterns. Check documentation consistency before creating a PR ( /check-docs → gh pr create hook) Vulnerability scan before pushing an image ( trivy image → docker push hook) Generate a coverage report before pushing ( go test -cover → git push hook) Ensure E2E tests have just been re-run before merging a PR ( pnpm test:e2e → gh pr merge hook) How It Works: Managing State with Markers Let's look at what the "marker" we've been mentioning is actually made of. markgate works by saving the "state" at the time the target command (or task) succeeded as a marker, and on the next call of the same command (or task), if the marker matches the current state, the run is skipped; if not, it runs ( markgate run ) / blocks ( markgate verify ) . In practice, this "state" is a hash of the code content . You can choose between two hash targets: "a specific set of files" ( hash: files + include ) or "the repository's git status as a whole" ( hash: git-tree , the default). Either way, as long as the code content hasn't changed, the command is skipped . # First run: no marker yet, so pnpm build runs and a marker is saved on success $ markgate run -- pnpm build building... passed in 7.2s # Second run: no file changes → execution is skipped $ markgate run -- pnpm build # After editing a file: the marker is invalidated, so the command runs again $ echo '// fix typo' >> src/foo.ts $ markgate run -- pnpm build building... passed in 7.1s By default, the marker file is stored inside .git ( .git/markgate/default.json ), so you don't need to create a marker file yourself, and it isn't tracked by git even without an explicit .gitignore entry. (There's also an option to explicitly change the marker file path and share markers between local and CI; see the README for that.) Installation # Homebrew brew install go-to-k/tap/markgate # shell script curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/go-to-k/markgate/main/install.sh | bash # go install go install github.com/go-to-k/markgate/cmd/markgate@latest # mise (ubi backend) mise use "ubi:go-to-k/markgate@0.3.3" Using markgate from Other Hook Managers So far I've used the Claude Code hook as the example, but markgate is hook-manager agnostic . With husky / lefthook / the pre-commit framework, or any other hook manager, you can use it just by writing a single line of markgate run -- . # .husky/pre-commit markgate run -- pnpm test # lefthook.yml pre-commit : commands : check : run : markgate run -- pnpm test # .pre-commit-config.yaml (pre-commit framework) repos : - repo : local hooks : - id : markgate-check name : markgate check entry : markgate run -- pnpm test language : system pass_filenames : false Final Thoughts Personally, I think this has turned into a tool I'll lean on in the AI era. In particular, the idea of "mechanically catching AI mistakes and omissions" feels like one of the important points when working with AI. For the other features ( exclude / state_dir settings in .markgate.yml , sharing markers between local and CI, strict gate dependencies via requires , etc.), see the README in the GitHub repository . If you like it, I'd be glad if you'd give the repository a ⭐.
