items.summary_html:
I built an OSS tool called markgate that mechanically catches and enforces two kinds of gaps: when a Coding Agent (Claude Code, etc.) accidentally forgets to call a Skill that runs build or tests after implementation and commits anyway, and when AI tasks that can't be reduced to a command — like a /check-docs Skill — can't be enforced through hooks.

markgate

NOTE: markgate is meant to run inside a git repository.

markgate

markgate is a CLI tool that acts as an enforcement layer wedged between the Coding Agent and your hooks. By mechanically catching and enforcing the Coding Agent's mistakes and omissions, it addresses the following three failure patterns.

Pattern Failure pattern it addresses Solution 1 Catching forgotten calls and avoiding duplicate execution markgate run 2 Enforcing non-command tasks markgate set + markgate verify 3 Scoping multiple tasks + aggregate verify composes in .markgate.yml

Below, we'll walk through each pattern in turn.

Pattern 1: Catching Forgotten Calls and Avoiding Duplicate Execution (markgate run)

Suppose you have an implementation skill, and a check skill (/check) that runs after it.

/check runs verifications against the implemented code. The things you want to guarantee against your implementation will vary by project — tests, typecheck, lint, format, build, documentation consistency, coverage generation, image scans, and so on.

However, even if you tell the Coding Agent "run /check after implementing", the Coding Agent can forget and silently skip the step. When that happens, your code gets committed without the checks you wanted to run.

So, you set up a pre-commit hook to forcibly run the equivalent of /check.

But the Coding Agent doesn't always forget. In fact, forgetting is rare — usually it runs /check just fine.

That leads to "the skill already ran it → the hook runs it again", a duplicate execution.

If /check is heavy, this slows down what should be a fast Coding Agent development cycle. If it's light you might not notice, but running it frequently still wastes a non-trivial amount of time.

Furthermore, if you skip the check after the implementation skill and put all check logic only in the hook, you can't run checks when you're not yet ready to commit. Running a post-edit hook on every file change isn't a great answer either, since the checks then run on every edit and that takes time.

Solved with markgate run

markgate keeps both the /check skill and the hook in place, and makes it so that the hook fires only when the Coding Agent forgets /check.

In other words, when the Coding Agent runs /check properly, the hook is skipped, so duplicate execution doesn't happen.

Usage

The basic flow is no config file required — just call the command.

For example, suppose your /check skill and pre-commit hook from above both run pnpm build. And suppose the pre-commit hook is wired up via Claude Code's PreToolUse hook firing on git commit*.

1. /check skill

In the /check skill that runs first, wrap the pnpm build command using markgate run -- .

// ... inside the skill definition
- pnpm build
+ markgate run -- pnpm build
2. hook

In the pre-commit hook, rewrite pnpm build to markgate run -- pnpm build in the same way.

{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [{
      "matcher": "Bash",
      "if": "Bash(git commit*)",
-     "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "pnpm build" }]
+     "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "markgate run -- pnpm build" }]
    }]
  }
}

With just this, you get the behavior where the hook fires only when the Coding Agent forgets /check, running pnpm build. When the Coding Agent runs /check properly, the latter hook is skipped, so duplicate execution doesn't happen.

Pattern 2: Enforcing Non-command Tasks (set + verify)

Up to this point, markgate run has meant writing the target command (pnpm build, etc.) directly into the hook configuration.

In practice, though, there are also tasks that can't be reduced to a command. For example, "is the documentation consistent with src?", "does the PR description match the diff?", "is naming consistent with the existing code?" — these are reviews that need LLM judgment and can't be expressed as a shell command.

You want to run this kind of LLM task in the Coding Agent's own session, because you want to leverage the context the Coding Agent has built up (conversation history, open files, past decisions). Technically, you could launch a separate session from a hook via claude -p, but since the context isn't shared, it doesn't act as a continuation of the work so far. As a result, the hook alone can't tell whether the Coding Agent ran an LLM task like /check-docs, which means there's no way to enforce it.

Building a Gate with set + verify

That's where the gate pattern — combining markgate set and markgate verify — comes in. The check itself stays on the skill side; set records "the moment the check passed" as a marker, and on the hook side, verify acts as a gate that judges whether "the recorded marker matches the current marker".

  • markgate set: records the moment the check passed as a marker
  • markgate verify: exits 0 if the recorded marker matches the current marker, and exits 1 to stop things if they don't match

Since the marker records the code state at the time of set, when the code changes afterward the recorded marker and the current marker no longer match, and verify stops things (we'll cover what's inside a marker later).

Usage

At the end of where the check actually runs (a skill like /check-docs), call markgate set. On the hook side, just call markgate verify.

# At the end of the /check-docs skill definition
markgate set

// .claude/settings.json (hook side)
{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Bash",
        "if": "Bash(git commit*)",
        "hooks": [
          { "type": "command", "command": "markgate verify || { echo 'run /check-docs' >&2; exit 1; }" }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}

The whole chain of check operations stays defined on the skill side, and the hook just looks at the marker. If the marker is missing or doesn't match the code, the hook blocks with exit 1, and the Coding Agent gets both the error and a hint (run /check-docs), so when the gate blocks things, recovery can be left to the Coding Agent and it can loop again.

Catching Both "First-time Non-command Triggers" and "Slip-ups"

This gate pattern is effective in both of the following cases.

  1. First-time non-command trigger: The Coding Agent doesn't even know /check-docs exists and tries to commit. → Since there's no marker, the hook blocks, and after reading the error message (run /check-docs), the Coding Agent runs /check-docs for the first time.
  2. Slip-up: The Coding Agent runs /check-docs and the marker is set. But later, when the code is edited again and you want to re-check, the Coding Agent forgets to re-run /check-docs. → Since the marker no longer matches the code, the hook blocks and prompts the Coding Agent to re-run.

In short, markgate uniformly catches both never-run-before cases and failure to re-run after a slip-up, using the same logic: "does the marker match the current code state?".

Pattern 3: Scoping and Aggregate Verify (.markgate.yml + composes)

So far we've assumed "one skill, one hook", but in practice you often have multiple checks lined up.

For example, suppose at pre-commit you want to run light checks (check: typecheck / lint / build / unit test) plus a heavier check that uses an LLM to verify documentation consistency (docs).

The problem here is wasted runs. If you bundle them into a single gate, even on a commit that only touches tests, the LLM consistency check runs even though nothing in the documentation-related files changed. That would mean re-running the heavy LLM check every time you change any code, which isn't practical.

Giving Each Task Its Own Scope

That's where .markgate.yml comes in: give each check its "own scope" (= the set of files specified in include). Whether a re-run is needed is judged by whether the code change falls within that scope.

On top of that, using composes to create an aggregate gate that bundles multiple gates means the hook side can judge "do all the bundled gates match the current code?" with just a single line of verify.

Usage

Create a .markgate.yml (markgate init generates a template).

# .markgate.yml
gates:
  check:
    hash: files # only the files specified in include are hashed
    include:
      - "src/**"
      - "tests/**"
      - "package.json"
  docs:
    hash: files
    include:
      - "src/**" # changes in src also affect docs, so include in both
      - "docs/**"
      - "README.md"
  pre-commit:
    composes: [check, docs] # aggregate gate: AND of check and docs

From the skill side, specify the gate name as an argument and set each gate individually.

# At the end of the /check skill definition
pnpm typecheck && pnpm lint && pnpm test && markgate set check

# At the end of the /check-docs skill definition
markgate set docs

Then, in the pre-commit hook, verify the pre-commit aggregate gate in a single line. When it doesn't match, markgate status pre-commit shows "which gate doesn't match", and the Coding Agent reads that and re-loops the corresponding skill.

// .claude/settings.json
{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Bash",
        "if": "Bash(git commit*)",
        "hooks": [
          { "type": "command", "command": "markgate verify pre-commit || { markgate status pre-commit >&2; exit 1; }" }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}

The key point is that only the checks needed for the edited scope get re-run. Each gate's marker only hashes the files in its own include, so on a commit that only touches one side's scope, the other gate's marker stays the same as when it was set and still matches, meaning no re-run is needed.

For example, a commit that only modifies tests re-runs only the light checks; a commit that only touches files outside any include (CI config, etc.) skips both.

Edited files check docs Checks that need to re-run tests/** only stale fresh light checks only docs/** / README.md only fresh stale heavy check only src/** stale stale both None of the above (CI config, editor config, etc.) fresh fresh none (commit passes)

Note that the pre-commit aggregate gate in this example is designed without a command of its own; it just performs the AND judgment — fresh if all bundled gates are fresh, stale if any one is stale. This shape — without its own command — can't be written with markgate run (which wraps a single command); only the gate pattern (set + verify) can express it.

Other Use Case Examples

Beyond the basic usage above, markgate has various advanced patterns.

  • Check documentation consistency before creating a PR (/check-docs → gh pr create hook)
  • Vulnerability scan before pushing an image (trivy image → docker push hook)
  • Generate a coverage report before pushing (go test -cover → git push hook)
  • Ensure E2E tests have just been re-run before merging a PR (pnpm test:e2e → gh pr merge hook)
How It Works: Managing State with Markers

Let's look at what the "marker" we've been mentioning is actually made of.

markgate works by saving the "state" at the time the target command (or task) succeeded as a marker, and on the next call of the same command (or task), if the marker matches the current state, the run is skipped; if not, it runs (markgate run) / blocks (markgate verify).

In practice, this "state" is a hash of the code content. You can choose between two hash targets: "a specific set of files" (hash: files + include) or "the repository's git status as a whole" (hash: git-tree, the default). Either way, as long as the code content hasn't changed, the command is skipped.

# First run: no marker yet, so pnpm build runs and a marker is saved on success
$ markgate run -- pnpm build
building...
passed in 7.2s

# Second run: no file changes → execution is skipped
$ markgate run -- pnpm build

# After editing a file: the marker is invalidated, so the command runs again
$ echo '// fix typo' >> src/foo.ts
$ markgate run -- pnpm build
building...
passed in 7.1s

By default, the marker file is stored inside .git (.git/markgate/default.json), so you don't need to create a marker file yourself, and it isn't tracked by git even without an explicit .gitignore entry. (There's also an option to explicitly change the marker file path and share markers between local and CI; see the README for that.)

Installation 
# Homebrew
brew install go-to-k/tap/markgate

# shell script
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/go-to-k/markgate/main/install.sh | bash

# go install
go install github.com/go-to-k/markgate/cmd/markgate@latest

# mise (ubi backend)
mise use "ubi:go-to-k/markgate@0.3.3"
Using markgate from Other Hook Managers

So far I've used the Claude Code hook as the example, but markgate is hook-manager agnostic. With husky / lefthook / the pre-commit framework, or any other hook manager, you can use it just by writing a single line of markgate run -- .

# .husky/pre-commit
markgate run -- pnpm test

# lefthook.yml
pre-commit:
  commands:
    check:
      run: markgate run -- pnpm test

# .pre-commit-config.yaml (pre-commit framework)
repos:
  - repo: local
    hooks:
      - id: markgate-check
        name: markgate check
        entry: markgate run -- pnpm test
        language: system
        pass_filenames: false
Final Thoughts

Personally, I think this has turned into a tool I'll lean on in the AI era. In particular, the idea of "mechanically catching AI mistakes and omissions" feels like one of the important points when working with AI.

For the other features (exclude / state_dir settings in .markgate.yml, sharing markers between local and CI, strict gate dependencies via requires, etc.), see the README in the GitHub repository. If you like it, I'd be glad if you'd give the repository a ⭐.

Also, as a project that actually uses markgate in practice, there's cdkd (CDK Direct) — a from-scratch rewrite of the AWS CDK CLI that's made it blazingly fast. Nearly all of the implementation is delegated to a Coding Agent, and markgate mechanically backs that up against missed runs and non-command tasks. Take a look if you're interested.

items.title: What I Learned Using Free AI Coding Agents on a Real Portfolio (OpenCode and Kilo)
items.summary: I'm a student, and I built and kept improving my portfolio with free AI coding agents running in the VS Code terminal. I used OpenCode and later Kilo, both on free models. They saved me a lot of time, but they also got stuck, lied by accident, and once looked busy for a whole hour without doing anything. Here is what I learned, so you can skip my mistakes. 1. Ask for a read-only diagnosis first My mobile menu showed a dark overlay and an "X" button, but the menu links never appeared. My first prompt was "fix it", and the fix didn't work. What worked was splitting the job into two steps: First, read only. Do not change anything. Find where the mobile menu is rendered and tell me exactly why the panel is invisible, with the file and line number. Then fix it. When the agent has to name the real cause, it stops guessing. In my case the real cause was a previous commit that had removed the menu panel completely. 2. Keep every prompt small My long prompts that asked for five changes at once often ended with "not done in this session". Short prompts with one job each worked much better. A prompt template I now use: Change ONLY in . Do not touch anything else. Use only text that already exists. Do not invent new content. Do not commit or push. Run the typecheck at the end and tell me which lines you changed. 3. Always tell the agent not to commit or push Agents are happy to "help" by committing and pushing. I wanted to review every change first. So every prompt says: do not commit or push . I check git status and git diff myself, and then I commit. 4. Typecheck passing does not mean the build passes Several times the agent said "typecheck passed", and I still had problems after deploying. The typecheck only checks types. A real build can still fail, and a failed build on Vercel means your site stays on the old version. Ask for the build too, and when it uses environment variables, give them: $ env : PORT = "5180" ; $ env : BASE_PATH = "/" ; pnpm --filter @ workspace/ritika-portfolio build Before you ask "why is my change not live?", check the deployment status in the Vercel dashboard. 5. Don't let the agent test in a browser I once asked an agent to verify a fix with a headless browser. It spent an hour fighting spawn pnpm ENOENT on Windows and trying one workaround after another. Now my prompts say: "Do not test in a browser or start a dev server. Only run typecheck and build." I look at the page myself. 6. Watch out for Windows and PowerShell Agents often write bash commands. On Windows PowerShell I kept seeing errors like: && is not a valid statement separator (use ; instead) grep , tail and head are not recognized commands 2>/dev/null fails with a path error If your agent keeps hitting these, add a line like "I use Windows PowerShell, so use PowerShell syntax" to your prompt. 7. "Already implemented" needs checking A few times the agent answered "Already implemented, no changes needed". Sometimes that was true. Sometimes I wanted proof. I started asking it to name the file and line number of the change, and then I searched for that text in VS Code with Ctrl + F . If the agent can't point to a line, don't trust the claim. 8. Free models have limits Free agents can hit a daily limit, or ask you to sign in. Mine said "You need to sign in to use this model" in the middle of a task. Signing up with an email was free and took a couple of minutes. Be ready to switch tools, and never run two agents on the same folder at the same time, because they will edit the same files and cause conflicts. 9. Never paste secrets to an agent Don't paste API keys, tokens or your .env file into a prompt or a chat. Keep them in environment variables and in your host's secret settings. Before pushing, search the diff for words like key , secret , token and password . My simple workflow now Ask for a read-only diagnosis Ask for one small change Run git status and git diff --stat Run the build locally Test the page myself, on desktop and on a phone-sized window Commit with a clear message and push Check that the deployment is Ready Check the live site in an incognito tab Wrapping up AI agents are great helpers, but they are not a replacement for checking your own work. The more specific and small my prompts were, the better the results. You can see the portfolio I built here: ritika-rajput-portfolio.vercel.app . I also share videos on RitikaMoments . What is the biggest problem you ran into while coding with an AI agent?
items.summary_html:
I'm a student, and I built and kept improving my portfolio with free AI coding agents running in the VS Code terminal. I used OpenCode and later Kilo, both on free models.

They saved me a lot of time, but they also got stuck, lied by accident, and once looked busy for a whole hour without doing anything. Here is what I learned, so you can skip my mistakes.

1. Ask for a read-only diagnosis first

My mobile menu showed a dark overlay and an "X" button, but the menu links never appeared. My first prompt was "fix it", and the fix didn't work.

What worked was splitting the job into two steps:

First, read only. Do not change anything.
Find where the mobile menu is rendered and tell me exactly why the panel
is invisible, with the file and line number.
Then fix it.

When the agent has to name the real cause, it stops guessing. In my case the real cause was a previous commit that had removed the menu panel completely.

2. Keep every prompt small

My long prompts that asked for five changes at once often ended with "not done in this session". Short prompts with one job each worked much better.

A prompt template I now use:

Change ONLY  in .
Do not touch anything else.
Use only text that already exists. Do not invent new content.
Do not commit or push.
Run the typecheck at the end and tell me which lines you changed.
3. Always tell the agent not to commit or push

Agents are happy to "help" by committing and pushing. I wanted to review every change first. So every prompt says: do not commit or push. I check git status and git diff myself, and then I commit.

4. Typecheck passing does not mean the build passes

Several times the agent said "typecheck passed", and I still had problems after deploying. The typecheck only checks types. A real build can still fail, and a failed build on Vercel means your site stays on the old version.

Ask for the build too, and when it uses environment variables, give them:

$env:PORT="5180"; $env:BASE_PATH="/"; pnpm --filter @workspace/ritika-portfolio build

Before you ask "why is my change not live?", check the deployment status in the Vercel dashboard.

5. Don't let the agent test in a browser

I once asked an agent to verify a fix with a headless browser. It spent an hour fighting spawn pnpm ENOENT on Windows and trying one workaround after another. Now my prompts say: "Do not test in a browser or start a dev server. Only run typecheck and build." I look at the page myself.

6. Watch out for Windows and PowerShell

Agents often write bash commands. On Windows PowerShell I kept seeing errors like:

  • && is not a valid statement separator (use ; instead)
  • grep, tail and head are not recognized commands
  • 2>/dev/null fails with a path error

If your agent keeps hitting these, add a line like "I use Windows PowerShell, so use PowerShell syntax" to your prompt.

7. "Already implemented" needs checking

A few times the agent answered "Already implemented, no changes needed". Sometimes that was true. Sometimes I wanted proof. I started asking it to name the file and line number of the change, and then I searched for that text in VS Code with Ctrl + F. If the agent can't point to a line, don't trust the claim.

8. Free models have limits

Free agents can hit a daily limit, or ask you to sign in. Mine said "You need to sign in to use this model" in the middle of a task. Signing up with an email was free and took a couple of minutes. Be ready to switch tools, and never run two agents on the same folder at the same time, because they will edit the same files and cause conflicts.

9. Never paste secrets to an agent

Don't paste API keys, tokens or your .env file into a prompt or a chat. Keep them in environment variables and in your host's secret settings. Before pushing, search the diff for words like key, secret, token and password.

My simple workflow now
  1. Ask for a read-only diagnosis
  2. Ask for one small change
  3. Run git status and git diff --stat
  4. Run the build locally
  5. Test the page myself, on desktop and on a phone-sized window
  6. Commit with a clear message and push
  7. Check that the deployment is Ready
  8. Check the live site in an incognito tab
Wrapping up

AI agents are great helpers, but they are not a replacement for checking your own work. The more specific and small my prompts were, the better the results.

You can see the portfolio I built here: ritika-rajput-portfolio.vercel.app. I also share videos on RitikaMoments.

items.title: Arrowhead AI Launches Fletch Voice Model for Multilingual Customer Calls
items.summary: Bengaluru-based voice AI startup Arrowhead AI on October 30 launched Fletch, an in-house text-to-speech (TTS) model designed for multilingual customer conversations across India and Southeast Asia. The model is already deployed across live customer calls, powering more than one million calls per day, the company said. “Owning our voice layer means we can tune every millisecond and every emotion for how India and Southeast Asia actually speak,” said Devyani Gupta, Founder and CEO of Arrowhead AI. “Fletch is our first step towards voice AI that sounds like it belongs here: 14 languages, and it starts speaking in under 100 milliseconds. We want every customer to hear a conversation, not a machine,” she added. The company said that Fletch is designed to handle regional accents, code-mixed sentences and Indian proper nouns. According to Arrowhead AI, Fletch supports languages including English, Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Bengali, Malay and Indonesian, and can switch between languages within a sentence. The company added that the model also adapts its vocal tone to the context of a conversation, with 12 emotion styles, including empathetic, apologetic, calm and firm. The company claims that the model has been trained on thousands of hours of curated regional speech and recordings from professional voice artists . Arrowhead said Fletch operates at a reported latency of 80 milliseconds and begins generating speech in under 100 milliseconds. Arrowhead AI said Fletch is deployed across customer interactions involving collections, sales, renewals and inbound customer service. The company works with enterprises including Axis Bank, RBL Bank, IndusInd Bank, Tata 1mg, upGrad, KreditBee, Kissht and TVS Credit. According to Arrowhead, Fletch delivers approximately 30% better pronunciation accuracy on selected terms, including brand names, product names, customer names and Indian proper nouns. The company said the improvement can reduce instances in which customers ask voice agents to repeat themselves. Vengadanathan Srinivasan, Co-founder and CTO of Arrowhead AI, said, “We built on the latest research in speech generation and trained it on thousands of hours of regional speech, with real voice artists. The result runs at 80 milliseconds of latency and adjusts its tone to what’s being said.” Fletch is built on a DiTAR-based architecture adapted and trained by Arrowhead. The model operates alongside the company’s speech recognition system, language model and dedicated address model within its voice AI platform. Arrowhead is expanding Fletch’s capabilities across Southeast Asia, including support for Malay and Indonesian. The company plans to demonstrate the model at Singapore FinTech Festival 2026, scheduled for November 18–20 at Singapore EXPO.

items.title: Mark Cuban says he split rent with 5 roommates at 24. He shared the math and the floor plan.
items.summary: Mark Cuban lived with 5 roommates early in his career. Bloomberg/Getty Images Mark Cuban said his first apartment, which he shared with five roommates, cost $400 apiece in 2026. He shared the floor plan of his old pad in "The Village," a three-bedroom, two-bathroom apartment in Dallas. Cuban has often mentioned about the frugal mindset with which he saved up to launch his company. Mark Cuban might own several multimillion-dollar properties today, but he started his career in a cheap shared apartment. The billionaire former "Shark Tank" investor has been open about the broke student mindset that ruled his 20s and helped him launch his first business, MicroSolutions. In an X post on Sunday, he went into the nitty-gritty of just how frugal he had been. Cuban said that at age 24, he lived in an apartment in Dallas that, today, costs $2,388. He said he shared it with five roommates, and his share of the rent came to what would have been $400 in 2026. He shared the floor plan of his old apartment in a complex called "The Village." The floor plan showed a three-bedroom layout with two bathrooms, a dining room, living room, and a kitchen. It measured 1,350 square feet in total. For those who care. This is the same unit layout, same complex in the Village Apartments, the Hills. Updated. Price $2388. Same in 2026 dollars as when I lived there. Split 6 ways. $400. Maybe there are extra charges. Maybe they won’t let 6 guys in there ( we weren’t… pic.twitter.com/RcOEzxqMva — Mark Cuban (@mcuban) November 1, 2026 "Tbh, I didn't mind living with 5 roommates. We all were in the same boat," he wrote. "I moved in when I was 24. Lived there or across the way for 2 years before I only needed one roommate." He told Forbes in a 2013 article that because he had been the last to move into the apartment, he didn't have a bed, a closet, or a dresser, and slept on the floor with his clothes stacked in a corner. Cuban's post about his former apartment was one of many about him weighing in on the cost-of-living crisis in the US. He responded to a comment asking him how someone working at a McDonald's can afford rent and other living expenses. In an earlier post, he wrote about working as a barback earning $2.15 an hour, living off canned food and happy-hour peanuts, and getting fired from a retail job he used to work at. "If it's not the lifestyle for you. So be it. If you don't think just getting any job to get started is the right career choice for you. Do what you think is right," Cuban, 68, wrote. Cuban often posts advice for early-career professionals on X about topics such as which companies to work at as AI-native new graduates , how to live frugally , and the questions to ask when deciding whether to stay at or leave a company. Mark Cuban might own several multimillion-dollar properties today, but he started his career in a cheap shared apartment.

The billionaire former "Shark Tank" investor has been open about the broke student mindset that ruled his 20s and helped him launch his first business, MicroSolutions. In an X post on Sunday, he went into the nitty-gritty of just how frugal he had been.

Cuban said that at age 24, he lived in an apartment in Dallas that, today, costs $2,388. He said he shared it with five roommates, and his share of the rent came to what would have been $400 in 2026.

He shared the floor plan of his old apartment in a complex called "The Village." The floor plan showed a three-bedroom layout with two bathrooms, a dining room, living room, and a kitchen. It measured 1,350 square feet in total.

For those who care. This is the same unit layout, same complex in the Village Apartments, the Hills. Updated.

Price $2388. Same in 2026 dollars as when I lived there. Split 6 ways. $400.

Maybe there are extra charges. Maybe they won’t let 6 guys in there ( we weren’t… pic.twitter.com/RcOEzxqMva

— Mark Cuban (@mcuban) November 1, 2026

"Tbh, I didn't mind living with 5 roommates. We all were in the same boat," he wrote. "I moved in when I was 24. Lived there or across the way for 2 years before I only needed one roommate."

He told Forbes in a 2013 article that because he had been the last to move into the apartment, he didn't have a bed, a closet, or a dresser, and slept on the floor with his clothes stacked in a corner.

Cuban's post about his former apartment was one of many about him weighing in on the cost-of-living crisis in the US. He responded to a comment asking him how someone working at a McDonald's can afford rent and other living expenses.

In an earlier post, he wrote about working as a barback earning $2.15 an hour, living off canned food and happy-hour peanuts, and getting fired from a retail job he used to work at.

"If it's not the lifestyle for you. So be it. If you don't think just getting any job to get started is the right career choice for you. Do what you think is right," Cuban, 68, wrote.

items.title: Li$^{2}$SAO: Lifting Light Singl-Rollout Asynchronous RL Optimization via Group-Relative Actor-Critic Bootstrapping
items.summary: Asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) is becoming a mainstream paradigm for post-training large language models (LLMs), as it improves training efficiency by updating the model as rollouts arrive. Recent work argues that group-wise sampling in GRPO does not naturally fit asynchronous RL training because rollout lengths follow a long-tailed distribution, and proposes Single-rollout Asynchronous Optimization (SAO) to improve stability and off-policy behavior, especially on agentic tasks. However, SAO relies on a closed-source value model obtained from scaling value pretraining. In this paper, we analyze GRPO and LiSAO, our lightweight reproduction of SAO without the pretrained value model, on single-turn reasoning and multi-turn agentic tasks. We find that GRPO outperforms LiSAO on reasoning tasks, while the reverse holds on agentic tasks. Since the value model of LiSAO is not yet well trained , LiSAO lags behind GRPO substantially in early training steps. To address this issue, we propose Li$^{2}$SAO, which Lifts Light Single-rollout Asynchronous Optimization with group-relative actor-critic bootstrapping: while the critic is cold, a group-relative advantage trains the actor and a group-centered return trains the critic, after which training switches to single-rollout GAE. Experiments show that Li$^{2}$SAO catches up with or surpasses GRPO in early training and further raises the later performance ceiling. Code is available at https://github.com/jd-cc-coder/Li2SAO.

items.title: Mage-VL-Cowork: A Full Training Recipe to Learn Hybrid Computer Use From Evolved Harnesses
items.summary: Effective computer-use agents (CUAs) should seamlessly combine visual GUI interaction with code and terminal execution within a single policy. We present Mage-VL-Cowork, a 4B hybrid CUA trained from a general multimodally aligned checkpoint through an end-to-end, progressive five-stage curriculum across midtraining, SFT, and RL. To power this curriculum at scale, Mage-CUA-Forge replaces per-task agent construction with reusable, skill-conditioned generation workflows and application-specific preparers, synthesizing 293,806 desktop and web tasks across 6,915 skills while reducing recurring per-task expenditure by 82.6%. Rather than directly distilling a default teacher, we evolve the teacher harness and instantiate specialized CUA harnesses to yield high-quality trajectories alongside stage-specific supervision. Mage-VL-Cowork-4B finally climbs to 66.0% on OSWorld-Verified through different training stages with more efficient reasoning cost, achieving state-of-the-art performance at its parameter size and pushing forward the frontier of on-device intelligence.

items.title: The Generative Gap Between Speculative Drafter and Continuous Diffusion Language Model
items.summary: Continuous diffusion language models (CDLMs) and speculative drafters offer efficient language generation but are typically evaluated differently: CDLMs generate independently through iterative refinement, whereas drafters propose text for target-model verification and correction. We compare their architectures without verification, using LangFlow for CDLMs and adapting DSpark's Markov and recurrent-head architectures for standalone generation. All models are trained from scratch for unconditional, single-block OpenWebText generation at lengths 16, 128, and 1024, without target features or verification, using common preprocessing, backbone dimensions, and training-update budgets. We evaluate generation perplexity (GenPPL) with an external language model and distributional similarity to reference text with MAUVE. With default denoising steps equal to sequence length, LangFlow outperforms both DSpark variants on both metrics at lengths 128 and 1024, while DSpark-RNN leads at 16. A conditional KL analysis characterizes dependencies excluded by the Markov head's previous-token conditioning. Recurrent memory removes this restriction and improves both metrics, but the longer-sequence gap persists. Teacher probability matching further lowers Markov GenPPL without observed MAUVE gains. Increasing LangFlow's denoising steps at fixed weights improves both metrics at lengths 16 and 128, changing the length-128 ordering relative to DSpark-RNN. These results establish LangFlow's longer-sequence advantage under the evaluated budgets and highlight iterative full-sequence refinement as a route to improving standalone generation beyond gains from recurrent head memory.

items.title: Qistas: A Pre-Registered, Portable Protocol for Fairness Evaluation of Large Language Models
items.summary: Fairness benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) are overwhelmingly English-born and American in their social categories; translated versions carry those categories into societies where they do not apply, and almost none fix their hypotheses before the models are run. We present Qistas (Arabic qistas, "the just balance"), a protocol for evaluating how LLMs treat the social, confessional, and regional constituencies of a society, portable across countries and instantiated first for Iraq. In its pilot form it measures only what needs no verdict on contested truth: procedural symmetry across matched counterfactual pairs, differential refusal, stereotype reliance under ambiguity, and terminological framing of documented events. Every measurement is paired by construction and analysed with paired machinery (sign-flip permutation tests, exact McNemar tests, template-clustered bootstrap intervals, Holm-corrected families), with a power analysis that states, before any data exist, the smallest effect each axis can detect after the design effect of template clustering. We release the authoring apparatus (a pruned 3x5 taxonomy with four cells closed by design, per-type checklists, a cumulative rulings log, a structural audit, and a human review notebook) and report its first field test: a semantic review of a 58-item seed bank in which 24 of 25 template groups failed at least one check. The defect patterns it exposed (evaluation criteria leaking into prompts, token-level swaps that break Arabic agreement, epistemically unbalanced pairs, single-theme refusal probes, unwritten dialect twins counted as coverage) are, we argue, general hazards of counterfactual fairness benchmarks. This is a protocol paper, not a results paper: no model has been evaluated, and the accompanying pre-registration commits the hypotheses, metrics, exclusion rules, and analysis plan that the pilot will follow.

items.title: CoFiBreak: A Coarse-to-Fine Diversity Reward for Effective Multi-Turn Jailbreak
items.summary: Automated red teaming trains an attacker large language model (LLM) to elicit harmful responses from a victim LLM, but reinforcement learning can collapse attackers onto a narrow set of prompts when attack success is the only reward. Such a collapse of attack diversity can bias safety evaluation toward repeatedly testing near-duplicate attack patterns rather than the underlying harmful intents. Existing methods often trade off attack success or inference cost for greater content or strategy diversity. We propose CoFiBreak, a coarse-to-fine diversity reward for Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) that improves attack diversity while preserving strong attack effectiveness and low inference cost. The coarse reward broadens which strategies the attacker uses by encouraging strategies underrepresented within each GRPO group, while the fine reward broadens how those strategies are realized by discouraging reuse of the same personas, framings, and output formats after harmful-intent information is removed from prompt embeddings. Diversity rewards apply only to attacks that already exceed an effectiveness threshold, so diversity cannot be gained through ineffective attacks. Since both rewards are computed only during training, CoFiBreak also retains inference efficiency. Trained with Llama3.1-8B-Instruct as the victim, CoFiBreak discovers 1.6-2.0x as many distinct successful fine-grained strategies as the strongest baseline across frontier victims on HarmBench. It reaches 98.8% ASR@10 (attack success rate with 10 generations per intent) on AdvBench with the highest diversity score among all compared methods, which is 2.1x that of the strongest-attacking baseline. The resulting attacks transfer to unseen frontier LLMs, reaching 71.0% ASR@10 on AdvBench with the unseen victim Claude-Opus-4.6. The code will be released.

Abstract: Automated red teaming trains an attacker large language model (LLM) to elicit harmful responses from a victim LLM, but reinforcement learning can collapse attackers onto a narrow set of prompts when attack success is the only reward. Such a collapse of attack diversity can bias safety evaluation toward repeatedly testing near-duplicate attack patterns rather than the underlying harmful intents. Existing methods often trade off attack success or inference cost for greater content or strategy diversity. We propose CoFiBreak, a coarse-to-fine diversity reward for Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) that improves attack diversity while preserving strong attack effectiveness and low inference cost. The coarse reward broadens which strategies the attacker uses by encouraging strategies underrepresented within each GRPO group, while the fine reward broadens how those strategies are realized by discouraging reuse of the same personas, framings, and output formats after harmful-intent information is removed from prompt embeddings. Diversity rewards apply only to attacks that already exceed an effectiveness threshold, so diversity cannot be gained through ineffective attacks. Since both rewards are computed only during training, CoFiBreak also retains inference efficiency. Trained with Llama3.1-8B-Instruct as the victim, CoFiBreak discovers 1.6-2.0x as many distinct successful fine-grained strategies as the strongest baseline across frontier victims on HarmBench. It reaches 98.8% ASR@10 (attack success rate with 10 generations per intent) on AdvBench with the highest diversity score among all compared methods, which is 2.1x that of the strongest-attacking baseline. The resulting attacks transfer to unseen frontier LLMs, reaching 71.0% ASR@10 on AdvBench with the unseen victim Claude-Opus-4.6. The code will be released.

items.title: Adaptive Personalization Under Preference Epistemic Uncertainty
items.summary: Human preferences change over time: an established preference may remain valid over time, become uncertain as context shifts, or be explicitly revised. Effective personalization requires conversational AI to adapt its response strategy to evolving preferences rather than relying on passive memory retrieval. We formalize this capability as adaptive personalization under epistemic uncertainty. A human preference study further confirms that people favor state-contingent response strategies as preference uncertainty changes. To evaluate whether language models mirror this adaptation, we create a multilingual benchmark spanning 250 personas, 5 languages, and 25K conversational turns that decouples strategy selection from response execution. Across eight closed- and open-weight models, we uncover a recognition-generation gap: models reliably identify appropriate strategies when selecting among candidate options, but collapse during open-ended generation, suffering a 35-46% drop in strategy calibration. Crucially, this failure is systematic: models default to exploit-first behavior, over-relying on existing preferences regardless of preference epistemic uncertainty. We show this failure is addressable: while prompting interventions fail, targeted training that supervises models' internal strategy representations toward state-conditional human preferences narrows the user acceptability generalization gap by a third on out-of-distribution personas and conversational styles.

items.title: Better Retrievers, Worse Labels: How Incomplete Relevance Judgments Distort Abstention Evaluation in Conversational RAG
items.summary: Conversational RAG benchmarks such as MTRAG and RETECO evaluate retrieval and generation end to end: each system answers from its own retrieval, so abstention must be scored against whether each retrieved context is sufficient. A convenient shortcut reads sufficiency off the relevance judgments and treats a context without gold documents as unanswerable. We re-run the official baselines exactly and test this shortcut on RECOR (RETECO track~2) with four retrievers (nDCG@10 from .18 to .59) and three Qwen3 readers. Two open LLM judges and a panel of four small open models label each context by content, and a model of another family audits 250 contexts blind, with adjudication. The stronger the retriever, the larger the share of no-gold contexts that still contain the answer (28\% to 72\%) and the lower the shortcut's precision (.68 to .10; .70 to .21 under the audit). A reader agrees: Qwen3-4B answers 62--67\% of these false misses correctly, against 23--30\% of no-gold contexts judged insufficient and 1\% with no documents. In most false misses, the answer comes from a hard negative mined for the same question, another turn's gold or a neighbouring chunk of the gold page. On MTRAG, whose judgments come from annotators, precision drops from .72 to .50. Under the shortcut, answerability AUROC is up to .19 too low, and the best sufficiency detector appears to be a retrieval score that never reads the documents. We release code, runs and labels, and recommend scoring refusals against content labels, not the presence of gold.

items.title: Fewer Heads, Fewer Memories: Pruning Redundant Attention Heads Suppresses Verbatim Memorisation
items.summary: Large language models have been shown to memorise and reproduce verbatim sequences from their training data, raising concerns about privacy leakage, intellectual property exposure, and the limits of generalisation. Recent theoretical work suggests that attention heads may contribute to this behaviour by functioning as associative memory mechanisms, with memorisation capacity scaling with the number of heads. At the same time, empirical work has shown that many attention heads are redundant and can be pruned with limited impact on downstream performance. Despite these parallel findings, the effect of pruning redundant heads on memorised-sequence reproduction remains unexplored. In this work, we demonstrate that zeroing out a substantial fraction of attention heads prior to inference can significantly suppress verbatim memorisation while preserving, or even improving, language modelling performance on the benchmark used to identify redundant heads. Evaluating GPT-2-XL(1.5B) on known memorised sequences, we find that pruning 729 task-redundant heads reduces the memorisation count by 91.5%, while improving WikiText-103 perplexity by 0.92. These findings suggest that attention-head redundancy can be exploited to mitigate memorisation at inference time, without retraining or modifying the training data.

items.title: Do Open Language Models Invent Scripture? BILAL-BENCH: Benchmarking Islamic-Source Fabrication in Bengali
items.summary: When a language model invents a Qur'anic verse or hadith, it gives false authority to text that readers may treat as sacred. Existing Islamic hallucination benchmarks are largely Arabic and often closed-ended, while Bengali resources mainly study general-domain hallucination or factual knowledge. We introduce BILAL-BENCH, a 240-question expert-verified benchmark for open-ended Islamic-source fabrication in Bengali. It covers Qur'anic attribution, hadith, fiqh, contemporary issues, and adversarial false-premise prompts, and uses a two-axis rubric that separates source errors from assertiveness. We evaluate seven open-weight models from 1B to 120B on 1,680 double-annotated responses. Six of the seven models confidently fabricate on 79.3-95.3% of source-production questions, with no monotonic improvement from scale. Hadith provenance is the weakest category across models: only two of 315 responses are correct and correctly sourced. The two 8B BanglaLLaMA variants have similar confident-fabrication rates but different error profiles. Models vary far more in whether they withhold a claim they cannot support than in source accuracy: appropriate abstention or false-premise correction ranges from 6 to 46 responses across the benchmark, and does not track parameter count.

items.title: Language Models Show Conformity Bias in RAG: When the Majority Endorses a Poisoned Claim
items.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can expose language models to misleading evidence in retrieved documents. We investigate whether increasing the number of mutually agreeing poisoned documents affects a model's ability to detect misinformation. We evaluate 200 randomly selected questions from SciFact (random seed 38), comparing contexts with one poisoned and six healthy documents against contexts with six mutually agreeing poisoned documents and one healthy document. For Gemma-3-12b, poison-detection rates decrease from 25% (50/200) in the minority condition to 10% (20/200) in the majority condition. Among the 38 questions with different outcomes across conditions, 34 change from detected to undetected, while only four change in the opposite direction (exact McNemar test, p = 6.04e-7). This pattern is consistent with a conformity-like response to a majority of mutually agreeing poisoned documents. Our results provide initial evidence of conformity bias in RAG-based misinformation detection: Gemma-3-12b is substantially less likely to detect poisoned claims when they dominate the retrieved evidence.

items.title: EDU-Jev Training System-One Decision Models for Education
items.summary: Many automated decisions in education involve choosing from a fixed set of options: assigning a rubric score, checking whether an answer meets a marking criterion, or identifying the first wrong step in a solution. Generative language models are increasingly used to make these decisions, but their responses require parsing, longer outputs increase inference costs, and confidence expressed in words does not necessarily reflect the probability of being correct. We present EDU-Jev, a family of single-pass ("System One") decision models at 0.8B, 2B and 4B parameters. Given an assessment context and a question with predefined answer options, the model returns a probability distribution over those options without generating text. A pointer head scores a marker for each option, ensuring the predictions are restricted to the allowed choices. Training uses a single supervised stage with soft cross-entropy against the available target label distributions; calibration is assessed empirically. Across twelve education benchmarks, EDU-Jev 4B achieves an average accuracy of 67.6%, exceeding the strongest of five commercial decision APIs by 9.4 percentage points and the best open 4B decision model by 18.7 points. On four cross-domain education sets, it matches the strongest API, which remains ahead on general decision-making and reasoning tasks. The 2B model processes about 150 decisions per second on a single H100 GPU.

items.title: Language Models Show a "Women-Are-Wonderful" Effect in Blame Attribution That is Not Just Leniency
items.summary: This paper investigates the Women-Are-Wonderful (WaW) effect in language-model blame attribution: a favorable bias in which women receive more positive evaluations than men. Using 11,270 interpersonal conflicts from r/AmItheAsshole, we construct matched counterfactuals that vary the gender of the person being judged (the original poster) and the person affected (the counter-party). Across four language models, gender changes a minority of verdicts, but those changes consistently favor women. The effect is strongly role-dependent. Making the original poster a woman reduces the odds of blame by 9--52%, while making the counter-party a woman multiplies them by 2.7--9.2X. Counter-party WaW also varies across conflict types, strengthening in communication and relationship conflicts and weakening in family conflicts. Exploratory probes suggest that counter-party gender can shift judgments of sympathy, reasonableness, harm and protection. WaW is therefore not just leniency toward women being judged: models also judge conduct more harshly when it affects a woman.

items.title: HyperRepair: Recovering Forgotten General Capabilities of Fine-Tuned Language Models
items.summary: Fine-tuning improves a language model's performance in a target domain but can weaken its general capabilities. Existing methods often face a trade-off between general capabilities and domain specialization, making it difficult to preserve both. We introduce HyperRepair, a framework for recovering general capabilities while retaining domain specialization at only inference cost. To make recovery generalizable across models sharing a pretrained backbone, HyperRepair learns a hypernetwork from repairs trained on source models. The hypernetwork uses activation fingerprints that summarize changes from the pretrained backbone to generate a tailored Repairing Side Net (RSN), whose prompt-conditioned gate applies corrections selectively. This enables recovery on models from unseen adaptation domains without target-domain examples or additional optimization. We evaluate HyperRpair across two model families, 12 LoRA adaptation datasets, and 15 general benchmarks. On the default split, HyperRepair achieves 93.4% of the base models' average general score while retaining 99.5% of the fine-tuned models' average domain score.

items.title: S2TDR: Structured Multimodal Reconstruction for Sticker-Aware Dialogue Understanding
items.summary: Stickers are widely used in social media dialogues to express affect, stance, and intent beyond literal text. Their meanings are often non-literal and context-dependent, making them difficult to handle with generic visual fusion or standalone captioning. We propose Sticker-to-Text Dialogue Reconstruction (S2TDR), a structured multimodal reconstruction framework that converts sticker turns into contextually appropriate textual utterances. S2TDR decomposes sticker interpretation into visual cue extraction, affective-intent inference, and context-aware dialogue reconstruction, using OCR text only as an auxiliary cue when available. The reconstructed dialogue can then be consumed by existing text-based dialogue models. Experiments on sentiment analysis, intent recognition, and dialogue summarization show that S2TDR generally improves multiple downstream models over direct sticker integration methods. Further analyses on component ablations, OCR-empty stickers, and reconstruction quality indicate that structured reconstruction provides an interpretable and effective way to integrate sticker semantics into dialogue understanding.

items.title: TraceSpec: Understanding and Improving Speculative Decoding for LLM Agents
items.summary: LLM agents execute tasks through repeated model calls over evolving histories of reasoning, actions, and tool feedback. Aggregate speculative-decoding metrics merge these distinct decisions, providing limited guidance on where draft supervision is needed. We present TraceSpec, a framework connecting trajectory evaluation with adaptive draft training. It combines dynamic execution with fixed-prefix replay and introduces TraceSpec-Traj, a corpus of 10,000 training states and 2,500 test states spanning browsing and software engineering. Analysis of five speculative baselines reveals that aggregate acceptance can rise with context length while declining within matched late browsing actions. Workload and phase further distinguish these trends, motivating supervision guided by trajectory conditions. TraceSpec trains on intermediate assistant turns and allocates a fixed prediction budget using state-conditioned estimates of prefix-aware acceptance gaps. Across three target sizes and two temperatures, it improves replay throughput by 12.5% to 22.6% over its DSpark base. Qwen3-4B ablations show that adaptive allocation increases accepted length by 3.3% to 10.0% over fixed full-turn supervision, with additional comparisons substantiating the roles of state conditioning and consecutive-token agreement. The resulting evaluation resources, trajectory findings, and training strategy connect the analysis of agent execution to practical draft improvement.

items.title: Beyond Response Scoring: An AI-aware Cognitive Supervision Framework for Automated Mathematical Short Answer Grading
items.summary: Transformer-based language models have achieved remarkable success in automated short answer grading (ASAG). However, current methods in ASAG struggle to comprehend, reason about and evaluate complex mathematical answers involving symbols and formulas. These score-only methods fail to generalize across diverse responses and skill states associated with identical scores. Moreover, they ignore the potential upward bias introduced by generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) usage in assessing students' performance and knowledge mastery. To address these limitations, we propose AICG (AI-aware Cognitive-supervised Grading), a two-branch multi-task framework. The first branch combines RoBERTa-based regression, ordinal, and classification heads for individual-answer grading. The second branch uses an expert-designed Q-matrix to associate responses with assessed skills and jointly predicts G-DINA-derived skill mastery and learning gain. Through the shared encoder, these skill-level targets provide cognitive supervision for answer grading beyond score labels. AICG further uses a Gen-AI detector, trained through supervised contrastive pretraining followed by linear classification, to estimate assistance probabilities and convert them into reliability weights, attenuating unreliable cognitive evidence during learning assessment. We conduct experiments on 49,402 instructor-graded responses spanning 19 academic semesters. Relative to RoBERTa regression, AICG reduces mean absolute error (MAE) by 50.3% and improves quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) from 0.798 to 0.927. Ablations identify Q-matrix-guided cognitive supervision as the primary source of improvement, while AI-aware weighting further reduces overall MAE by 4.2% over the unweighted cognitive model and consistently improves MAE and QWK across the four most recent post-Gen-AI semesters.

items.title: PsyInterviewee: Informational Invariance and Relational Adaptivity in Mental Health Interview Simulation
items.summary: LLM-based simulated interviewees support interviewer training and the evaluation of mental health interviewing systems. Existing studies have primarily focused on improving human-likeness through richer patient profiles and behavioral modeling. However, human-likeness alone does not establish their reliability. Reliable simulation requires preserving profile-grounded clinical facts (informational invariance) while adapting disclosure and interaction behavior to the interview (relational adaptivity). To this end, we introduce PsyInterviewee, which separates a protected truth channel from a dynamic interaction channel and verifies generated clinical claims against the profile. Specifically, asymmetric write permissions allow dialogue context to update disclosure and behavioral states without authorizing new clinical facts; these states guide what profile-supported information is revealed and how it is expressed. In an automated evaluation of interactions between LLM-based interviewers and interviewees, PsyInterviewee achieves higher scores than four representative baselines on most metrics across both axes, as assessed by two LLM judges. Ablations suggest that the two channels contribute to clinical grounding and response modulation, respectively.

items.title: In-Model Context Compression with Agentic Soft Tokens for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
items.summary: Long-horizon LLM agents play an important role in solving complex and sustained tasks, with ever-growing interaction contexts. However, these accumulated contexts will raise substantial computational cost and obscure key decision-relevant evidence. Existing methods typically train external compressors or context-management agents to rewrite context as shorter hard-token sequences, but such external selection may not align with the LLM's evolving representation and is necessarily lossy. In this paper, we introduce Agentic Soft-Token Compression (ASTC), a training-free compression method using soft tokens within LLM agent for long-horizon tasks. Specifically, ASTC uses the model's native recurrent dynamics to determine the already absorbed information, leveraging the commonly-used hybrid Gated Delta Network (GDN)-attention. It then carries this information forward as agentic soft tokens while retaining exact values as hard tokens. The resulting compact sequence reduces later-layer computation and yields reusable KV caches, extending the savings across the agent's trajectory. Extensive experiments on long-horizon tasks show that ASTC matches or exceeds the uncompressed agent's accuracy with up to 50.68% fewer end-to-end Attention Pairs, while trained compressors require 15.4 to 103.7 times more Attention Pairs per successful task. These findings highlight agentic soft tokens as a model-native way to carry absorbed context forward as the task representation evolves.

items.title: From Transcription to Reformulation: Defining and Benchmarking Grounded Generative Speech Recognition
items.summary: Speech language models have expanded automatic speech recognition (ASR) from transcription to general speech-to-text generation. Yet existing benchmarks still assume a single ground-truth transcript per utterance, an assumption that struggles when models produce readable, formatted, or structured outputs. In this work, we introduce Grounded Generative Speech Recognition (GSR), reformulating speech recognition as generating semantically grounded text instead of a single transcript. We define a grounded reformulation space that characterizes all valid textual realizations supported by the input speech, and establish a four-level hierarchy of reformulation capabilities, including literal transcription, canonical reformulation, semantic reformulation and speech-grounded structuring. Based on this formulation, we present GSR-Bench, the first comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate generative speech recognition systems beyond exact transcript matching. GSR-Bench covers diverse scenarios including refined meeting transcription, cross-dialect translation, context-aware speech understanding, and robustness under silent or noisy acoustic conditions. To address the limitations of word-level evaluation metrics, we develop a multi-dimensional evaluation framework combining speech grounding assessment and LLM-based semantic judgment, whose reliability is validated through human preference studies. Extensive experiments across representative architectures, ranging from conventional ASR systems to end-to-end Speech-LLMs, reveal fundamental trade-offs between transcription fidelity and generative reformulation ability. Our analysis further identifies critical failure modes, including acoustic hallucination, unsupported generation, and instruction drift, providing insights into the design and evaluation of future grounded generative speech systems.

items.title: Comparative Evaluation of LLM-Based Review Paradigms for Academic Paper Quality Assessment
items.summary: Growing submission volumes have renewed interest in using large language models (LLMs) to support peer review. It remains unclear how such evaluation should be structured, how much the model matters, and whether LLM scores predict research impact. We evaluate five paradigms across three input representations and three LLMs on 232 stratified ICLR 2025 submissions. Direct absolute rating matches comparative ranking on rank correlation with human scores, yet compresses most predictions above the accept threshold, flagging almost none of the papers reviewers scored below it. A base-rate-matched recalibration control locates the cause: comparative ranking supplies placement, not better ordering, and after recalibration Direct Rating reaches higher agreement than Elo while making 24% as many API calls. Abstract-only input beats full-paper summarization, and model choice matters as much as paradigm choice. Replicating on all 11,513 scored submissions reproduces these patterns, shows absolute agreement depends on the evaluated set's score spread, and finds none beating an always-reject baseline in accuracy. Human scores track citations better than any paradigm, with one exception: Group Rating retains its citation correlation after controlling for human scores, and alone ranks within the accepted pool. Ranking quality alone cannot assess review quality; calibration, thresholds, model, and target outcome all matter.

items.title: BlindToChange: AI Agents Can Find Changes When Asked But Do They Look When Needed?
items.summary: Given that AI agents can search the web broadly and deeply in real time, it is tempting to conclude that their outputs account for recent world events. We show that this conclusion does not hold in practice. While agents can search and easily find recent changes, the correctness of their responses depends on whether they search and what they search for. Popular agentic search benchmarks like BrowseComp cannot expose failures wherein agents do not recognize their own assumptions that should be verified, since these benchmarks explicitly state what needs to be found. In contrast, many user requests state only the final information need (e.g., an itinerary for a trip), leaving the agent to discover relevant changes (e.g., the temporary closure of a museum) and account for their consequences. To highlight such gaps, we introduce BlindToChange, a benchmark that measures whether agents proactively discover recent events that affect their responses. Our benchmark comprises requests for recommendations where an obvious candidate is no longer applicable due to a recent real-world event. These events are drawn automatically from Wikidata, allowing BlindToChange to be periodically refreshed. Strikingly, we find a big gap -- as high as 27.5 points, even at high reasoning effort -- in systems' performance, when the recent event is not explicitly mentioned compared to when we ask about it directly. Analyzing search trajectories, we learn that more than half of the failures can be attributed to the fact that agents do not directly search to verify whether a relevant fact has changed. Our benchmark highlights, and tracks, a new axis of progress, wherein systems account for recent information that is not explicitly mentioned in the user request.

items.title: KV-Cache Patching: Tracing How and Where Fine-Tuned Behaviors Arise
items.summary: Fine-tuning a language model changes how it responds, but where is this fine-tuned behavior instantiated? To better understand this, we evaluate whether the change in model behavior arises only during the generation of the answer tokens where the change manifests, or whether altered processing of previous tokens causes it via the attention mechanism. For this, we patch the KV cache from a LoRA fine-tuned model into the unmodified base model, and vice versa. Our results show that for some behaviors, like responding in German or emergent misalignment, patching the KV cache can indeed transfer them from the fine-tuned to the base model. Correspondingly, patching the KV cache from base to fine-tune can partially or fully remove fine-tuned behavior. Furthermore, we find that the effect of patching grows with how much of the KV cache is patched and concentrates at a few pivotal positions, with system-prompt and chat-template tokens having disproportionate influence.

items.title: KEEPER: Learning Control-Sufficient Textual Memory for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
items.summary: Recursive textual memory can carry earlier errors into later updates, yet task performance alone does not establish memory reliability. We define self-consistency bias as the persistence of incorrect claims already present in the incoming memory. We present KEEPER, a comparative analysis of four auxiliary objectives along information-content and update-sensitivity axes within a shared recursive interface, examining how supervision targets relate to agent performance. Among evaluated conditions, reward-related prediction achieve the highest task performance before and after offline reinforcement learning, outperforming joint supervision. A claim-level analysis of one baseline trajectory documents error persistence despite corrective observations. Together, these analyses motivate evaluating error persistence and valid-information retention alongside task outcomes.

items.title: Sparse Text Diffusion under Dual Budgets: Context Connectivity and Expert Activation
items.summary: Long-context diffusion repeatedly pays for both token interaction and feed-forward computation. We formulate these costs as two separate budgets: the edges available to an attention graph and the experts activated for each token. This view connects local, dilated, and global attention with conditional expert computation without assuming that sparsity alone preserves document-level information. We specify normalized masked attention, distinguish denoising depth from sampling iterations, and derive graph and compute bounds. A reported sparse-expert configuration, denoted DualBudget, is analyzed across scientific summarization, multi-hop question answering, dialogue, and sentence-pair prediction. All supplied table measurements are retained. The length study shows gains over the listed baselines through 16K, together with measurable degradation as length increases. Ablations reveal mixed changes across the three reported scores, while the cost record indicates a 20% reduction relative to DiffuSeq under an unspecified timing convention. The analysis separates these observations from unmeasured claims about training speed, absorbing states, global coherence, and deployment memory.

items.title: Enhancing Knowledge Entity Relation Extraction in Abstracts and Full-text Content of Academic Articles Using Large Language Models
items.summary: This study investigates the effectiveness of large pre-trained language models (LLMs) for knowledge entity relation extraction (KERE) from academic papers. Existing studies have examined individual types of LLM-based strategies and evaluated model performance using metrics such as precision and recall. To provide a broader evaluation, this study investigates multiple strategies, including closed-source LLM-based CoT prompting, LoRA-adapted open-source LLMs, LLM-enhanced small pre-trained language models (SLMs), and SLM-enhanced closed-source LLMs. In addition, this study introduces two strategies, namely SLM-enhanced open-source LLMs and closed-source LLM-enhanced open-source LLMs. These strategies are evaluated from multiple perspectives, including metrics, their ability to mitigate errors observed in SLMs, and potential directions for model optimization. This study manually constructs two annotated datasets in the NLP domain, covering Abstract and Full-Text datasets. Experimental results show that the LoRA-adapted T5 model achieves the highest macro F1 scores of 0.7408 and 0.7013 on the Abstract and Full-Text datasets, respectively. SLMs also benefit from LLM-generated entity descriptions under the LLM-enhanced SLM strategy. Error analysis further reveals that the effectiveness of LLM-based strategies in mitigating SLM errors varies across error types. Based on the identified limitations and error patterns of these strategies, several optimization directions are proposed. In addition, combining strategies with different error patterns further improves KERE performance.

items.title: CEFR Level Assessment across Languages and Text Granularities
items.summary: Automatic assessment of textual CEFR levels is an important task in educational natural language processing. However, accurate CEFR level prediction remains challenging due to the naturally imbalanced distribution of CEFR levels and the ambiguous boundaries between adjacent levels. To address these challenges, we propose a unified training objective that combines focal loss with supervised contrastive learning. Focal loss mitigates class imbalance by emphasizing underrepresented and difficult examples, while supervised contrastive learning learns more discriminative representations by encouraging intra-class compactness and inter-class separation. We evaluate the proposed method on sentence- and document-level CEFR assessment in both monolingual and multilingual settings. Experimental results demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms strong baselines across all settings, establishing new state-of-the-art performance on multiple CEFR assessment benchmarks.

items.title: Digital sovereignty in professional translation workflows: a case study of migrating from Windows to Linux
items.summary: This study examines digital sovereignty in professional translation through a screening of computer-assisted translation tools and translation management systems, and a case study of migrating a translator's workstation from Windows to Linux. The framework combines three principles - Control, Continuity and Exit - with three practical requirements: native Linux operation, independence from mandatory external services, and independent access to essential data and resources. Drawing on documentary evidence and the limited number of responses received from providers, the ecosystem screening distinguishes Linux accessibility from operational independence: browser-based platforms may remain dependent on provider-controlled infrastructure. The migration case demonstrates the feasibility of reconstructing one professional workflow around a locally operable Linux core, using LoopCAT, LibreOffice and locally run TranslateGemma, alongside tools for optical character recognition, communication, credential management and backup. Selected cloud services remained available where needed. The findings suggest that digital sovereignty depends on how workflow dependencies are organized, rather than on individual applications or operating systems. It does not require technological isolation, but meaningful control over essential components, continuity of work and practical exit options. The framework is tailored to the case examined here and may require adaptation to other professional workflows.

items.title: BYOD: Build Your Own DLM - Efficient Autoregressive-to-Diffusion Language Model Conversion
items.summary: Unlike autoregressive (AR) models, diffusion language models (DLMs) permit parallel token updates, flexible generation, and bidirectional attention, but leading systems rely on costly pretraining or full-model fine-tuning. We present Build Your Own DLM (BYOD), a generalizable LoRA-only recipe for parameter-efficient AR-to-DLM conversion. Without architecture-specific tuning, BYOD induces diffusion generation in Gemma 2 9B, Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen2.5 7B, and Ministral 8B; to our knowledge, this is the first reported AR-to-DLM conversion of a Mistral model. The adapters comprise 4.1-5.8% of final parameters while every base-model parameter remains frozen; each 25,000-iteration conversion needs at most 102.4M tokens, processed in 3.1-4.0 hours on one Google Colab GPU. All four models generate from fully masked sequences, use bidirectional context in a controlled attention test, and retain substantial parent-model knowledge. BYOD-Gemma is the strongest BYOD conversion on our nine-task evaluation, reaching 50.6% average accuracy compared with 51.9% for LLaDA 8B Instruct in the same harness. Open-generation quality at low network function evaluation (NFE) budgets remains the principal limitation: BYOD perplexity is 8.3-11.1 versus 4.1 for LLaDA and 2.2-3.0 for the AR parents when generating 128 tokens in 64 steps. To enable further experimentation and inspection, we provide a standalone training and evaluation implementation and interactive demos for all four conversions. BYOD thus provides a practical route for extending diffusion generation to other existing model families while identifying the gap that efficient conversion must next close.

items.title: Saidzoda-Tajik-LFM-2.6B: Adapting a 2.6B Hybrid Model to Tajik Tool Calling, and What Continued Pretraining Takes Away
items.summary: We release Saidzoda-Tajik-LFM-2.6B, a Tajik adaptation of the 2.6B-parameter hybrid model LFM2.5-2.6B-Base, built for tool calling in Tajik on modest hardware. The recipe has two stages: LoRA continued pretraining (CPT) on 1,485,319 cleaned Tajik web documents for 3 epochs, then one epoch of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on a mix of machine-translated Tajik tool calls, English tool calls kept as replay, and Tajik instructions. On a 174-item tool-calling test set built from BFCL v3 and machine-translated to Tajik, strict full-call accuracy on Tajik prompts rises from 20.69 for the base model to 64.14 (paired difference +43.45 points, 95% interval +35.2 to +51.7); a lenient parser that also accepts the base model's own call formats puts the base at 31.72. English shows no detectable change (76.55 and 77.24). Every CPT checkpoint scores zero: CPT removes the native tool-call format and, as the lenient re-scoring shows, part of the skill itself. Outside tool calling, accuracy on a Tajik knowledge benchmark rises from 28.0 to 35.0, Belebele Tajik shows no significant change, and English MMLU falls from 60.8 to 52.5. The model is not a general Tajik assistant. It almost never declines when no tool fits (6.9% correct on Tajik, against 31.0% for the base under the lenient parser), it is weak at multi-turn calls, and its calls should be checked before they are executed. We describe the data, the training settings and every evaluation in enough detail to repeat them.

items.title: When Steering Shifts Discourse: Identifying and Intervening on Discourse-Level Changes due to Activation Steering in LLMs
items.summary: Activation steering is an inference-time technique used to control or modify the behavior, tone, or safety properties of a large language model (LLM) without retraining the model's weights or editing its input prompt, but simply by adding a vector to its residual-stream activations. However, activation steering also changes the generated text in unintended ways, unrelated to intended behavior change, that are not well understood. Prior work has measured these changes only through coarse signals such as perplexity. We present a way of countering this by adding a second, complementary vector that targets the affected discourse dimension. items.title: Precision--Recall Trade-off on the Inference Level for LLMs in Grammatical Error Correction
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have recently been adopted for Grammatical Error Correction (GEC), achieving strong performance via both full fine-tuning and prompt-based approaches. As probabilistic sequence models, LLMs expose inference-time parameters that directly modify token generation behavior; however, their potential for controlling GEC-specific trade-offs has not been systematically studied. In this work, we investigate decoding strategies for grammatical error correction. We show that the repetition penalty parameter enables controllable adjustment of the precision--recall trade-off at inference time, without modifying the model architecture, training procedure, or prompt. Through experiments on standard GEC benchmarks, we demonstrate that repetition-penalty-based decoding enables inference-time control of the precision--recall balance, conceptually related to methods previously proposed for sequence-to-sequence GEC models, such as Align-and-Predict Decoding (APD), while remaining simple and broadly applicable to existing LLMs that expose inference-time decoding penalties.
