items.title: Cost-Aware Stopping for Freeze-Thaw Bayesian Optimization: When Does One-Step Lookahead Suffice?
items.summary: Freeze-thaw Bayesian optimization (BO) evaluates candidates in resumable increments but usually stops at a budget or convergence test. We maximize a budget-free utility, the best observed score minus a cost per increment, with a one-step lookahead: advance the candidate with the largest expected improvement (EI) under a fixed surrogate, and stop once no EI exceeds the cost. This rule, EI stopping, never falls below stopping immediately in expected utility, yet it can stop too early. We construct a certificate, a lower bound on the value of two-step lookahead, that proves such a stop premature, and repeating this correction never lowers expected utility under the surrogate. Under the surrogate, EI stops are premature on average at low costs and lose little at high costs. On three hyperparameter optimization benchmarks, a pre-registered test finds EI stopping noninferior to the correction in most high-cost settings, while the correction gains at low costs on two of the three; more information sharing in the surrogate raises EI stopping's utility. On the surrogates of two published methods, EI stopping trades lower scores for fewer training increments. EI stopping is a simple cost-aware reference whose utility depends on the surrogate.

items.title: Towards Understanding the Impact of Plasticity Loss on Reinforcement Learning in Stochastic Environments
items.summary: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) is a powerful framework for sequential decision-making. Despite many high-profile successes in recent years, deep RL is known to be brittle. An emerging line of research attributes this brittleness to a loss of plasticity in neural networks. However, plasticity loss has so far been understudied in stochastic environments. We study this interplay systematically, training SAC agents on three DeepMind Control tasks augmented with controlled levels of observation and action noise. We find that plasticity-preserving methods increase learning robustness on the two harder tasks, with their advantage growing as observation noise increases, while combining resets with layer normalization underperforms resets alone at every observation noise level tested. Further, stochasticity can accelerate the loss of plasticity in harder environments, whereas in easier settings noise can act as a regularizer that sustains plasticity. Lastly, plasticity loss is most pronounced in the early stages of training. In the most challenging stochastic settings, TD instability rather than gradual plasticity loss becomes the dominant failure mode.

items.title: Hyperbolic Inverse Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) seeks to infer the reward function underlying observed behavior, but its predictive accuracy and interpretability depend on how that reward is computed from the underlying features. While prior IRL reward functions have been implemented through a variety of techniques including linear weights, neural networks, or other function approximators, none make assumptions about the geometry of the underlying feature space. Inspired by geometric organization observed in neural circuits, we introduce Hyperbolic inverse reinforcement learning (Hyperbolic IRL), which parameterizes reward as a function of Hyperbolic distance between the feature vector and a learned parameter vector, as well as its Euclidean distance variant. We tested our methods against a range of linear and nonlinear IRL baselines under both deterministic and stochastic policies. Our Hyperbolic approach achieved comparable performance to state-of-the-art models on established benchmarks and excelled in the low data limit and across dense environments. Applied to human navigation among multiple exhibits in a museum room, Hyperbolic IRL reveals reward structure that depends not only on individual exhibit-distance features, but also on non-separable conjunctions between them. Together, these results demonstrate that a Hyperbolic reward parameterization can improve both the predictive accuracy and interpretability of IRL, providing a framework for studying how non-separable, conjunctive structure can begin to explain behavior.

items.title: Fast Privacy Loss Accounting for Random Allocation via Multiscale FFT
items.summary: In the random allocation sampling scheme each user's data is used in $k$ steps chosen randomly and uniformly from a sequence of $t$ steps. This scheme is known to improve on Poisson sampling in private optimization and in communication-efficient aggregation. The existing privacy loss distribution (PLD) accountant for this scheme runs in time quadratic in the inverse of the accuracy parameter $\alpha$ (Feldman and Shenfeld, 2026). We give an algorithm, \emph{multiscale FFT}, that represents likelihood ratios on a grid that is uniform within each dyadic interval and computes the exact rounding of every pairwise sum using FFTs within each interval. It keeps the guarantees of the accountant and improves the dependence of its running time on $\alpha$ from $O(\alpha^{-2})$ to $O(\alpha^{-1}\log(1/\alpha))$. In addition, we demonstrate that rounding can be performed via the mean-preserving connect-the-dots projection of (Doroshenko et al., 2026). This reduces the errors that rounding introduces in the mean of the privacy loss and in the $\chi^2$ divergence of the computed pair from the order of $\alpha$ to $O(\alpha^2/\log(t))$. In our experiments, our algorithm achieves speedups of several orders of magnitude at high accuracy and gives improved privacy bounds for DP-SGD with PREAMBLE.

items.title: Gradient Descent on Two ReLU Neurons: Global Landscape and Bifurcation Dynamics
items.summary: Understanding how gradient descent learns features remains a central challenge in neural network theory. We study this question in a minimal multi-index setting that already exhibits rich multi-phase gradient dynamics: a well-specified two-neuron ReLU teacher-student model under isotropic Gaussian inputs, trained by population gradient flow from small initialization. We show that the dynamics are organized by two directions: the "easy" bisector direction, which carries the leading signal, and the "hard" splitting direction, which governs specialization. To characterize the loss structure and learning behavior, we analyze the population squared-loss landscape and show that every critical point with both student weights nonzero is either a global minimum or a saddle. We then track the gradient-flow trajectory, showing that student neurons first collapse toward a bisector saddle before escaping and specializing to teacher neurons. Our results provide both a landscape and dynamics account of the multi-phase symmetry-breaking behavior that arises in a simple multi-index model and under standard algorithmic and architectural choices.

items.title: Physiological Trajectories and Observation Patterns in ICU Mortality Prediction: Transportability Under Changing Measurement Conditions
items.summary: Objective: To distinguish the transferable predictive value of physiological trajectories from that of observation patterns in ICU mortality prediction, and to assess whether measurement timing affects performance independently of observation quantity. Materials and Methods: In-hospital mortality was predicted at 48 hours using MIMIC-III, MIMIC-IV, and eICU. Nested representations progressively integrated latest-value snapshots (R1), longitudinal physiological summaries (R2), and measurement frequency and timing features (R3). Models fitted on 7,762 MetaVision patients were evaluated on 21,682 MIMIC-IV patients and 43,878 eICU patients across 204 hospitals. The effect of measurement timing was assessed while holding the number of retained observations constant. Results: Physiological trajectories improved external prediction in eICU (R2-R1 log-loss difference -0.00922, 95% CI -0.01148 to -0.00704). Observation-pattern features improved locally developed eICU models (R3-R2 -0.00257, 95% CI -0.00370 to -0.00146), but not clearly after transfer from MetaVision (-0.00012, 95% CI -0.00206 to +0.00208). R3 was favoured in 10 of 30 source bootstrap refits. At matched observation counts, retaining measurements spread throughout the window reduced log loss relative to random retention by 0.03280 for R3 versus 0.00703 for R2. Removing the final 12 hours increased log loss relative to count-matched random removal by 0.01947 for R3 versus 0.00822 for R2. Under reduced availability, the local R3 increment changed from beneficial to harmful. Discussion: Physiological trajectories transferred more consistently, while observation-pattern features were particularly sensitive to the timing and availability of measurements. Conclusion: Clinical prediction models should be evaluated not only in new patient populations but also under the measurement conditions that supply their inputs.

items.title: Instance-dependent sequential limits as an exact information ledger
items.summary: Instance-dependent limits for bandit regret, sequential tests, best-arm identification and Markov decision processes are proved by one chain. It runs from a divergence decomposition through data processing to a statistic, a testing step that turns a class guarantee into a requirement on the history, and optimization over alternatives and allocations. Only the first step is an identity. This work writes the chain as an exact ledger. By the chain rule, data processing loses exactly a conditional divergence, which vanishes for arms in natural exponential families at the per-arm counts and reward sums. A one-parameter family of martingale identities extends the decomposition to every tilt between two instances. The classical limits follow by relaxations with named defects. All defects but the asymptotic step's can be computed from an algorithm's own runs, the uniform quantification's only when the class guarantee is a number. On seven published sources, from movie ratings to engine replacement, the ledger locates the difference between standard algorithms and the classical limits. For identification among trained models and for Wald's test the largest term is usually the uniform quantification's.

items.title: Counting on Dummies: Privacy Amplification with Observable Counts and Truncated Batches
items.summary: In many practical deployments of Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (DP-SGD), the server processes data in batches. Randomly sampling these batches allows for better privacy bounds via privacy amplification results. Most sampling schemes with provable privacy amplification, including Poisson sampling and random allocation, result in variable batch sizes. The privacy guarantee of these schemes requires that the batch sizes are not revealed. In distributed settings, the server performing the aggregation or any party observing the communication traffic may learn these batch sizes. Furthermore, in both centralized and distributed settings, memory and computation constraints may require each batch to be of some maximum size $s$, necessitating truncation of the batch when it exceeds this limit. It is known that this truncation can result in a significant increase in privacy loss. In this work, we address both of these challenges via a simple mechanism that uses a random number of \emph{dummy points} to privatize the batch size and maintain the privacy guarantee even under truncation. We demonstrate that our mechanism is easy to implement in a distributed setting, and provide a general analysis of this mechanism for both Poisson sampling and random allocation. Our analysis is designed to support efficient and relatively tight privacy accounting. It also effectively amplifies the privacy of the count releases by subsampling, making the expected number of dummy points asymptotically smaller than what is needed to directly privatize the (sensitivity-one) batch sizes with non-negative noise. For Poisson sampling with truncated batches, we demonstrate empirically that our mechanism achieves better privacy--efficiency tradeoffs than the direct accounting for truncation recently given by (Ganesh, 2025).

items.title: India floats AI plan under which ‘The model travels to the data, rather than the data travelling to the model’
items.summary: As debate and legal argument continue over the extent to which developers of large language models are entitled to feed the world’s data into their systems without paying for it, India’s government has come up with an idea to regulate and secure the flow of information. India’s motive is to create AI models trained on local data, because it thinks offshore model-makers won’t be motivated to address the nation’s issues or to ensure owners of data stay in control. The scheme India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) thinks can make that happen is called the “Data Empowerment and Protection Architecture (DEPA) for AI Training.” As described by Professor Ajay Kumar Sood, Principal Scientific Adviser to the Government of India, DEPA means “the model travels to the data, rather than the data travelling to the model.” The scheme envisions “Training Data Providers” (TDPs) – examples of which include hospitals, banks, and government agencies – sharing anonymized and encrypted data with a “Data Exchange Platform” (DEP). Entities called “Training Data Consumers” (TDCs) access the data stored at the DEPs to train their models. DEPs will operate what MeitY calls “hardware-based Secure Data Environments” in which “data remains encrypted and isolated even during processing.” They also enforce rules set by TDPs that describe how TDCs can use data. MeitY’s DEPA framework [PDF] says this scheme means “Differential privacy techniques are systematically applied to prevent the model from learning or revealing individual specific information,” adding “All activities inside the secure data environments are immutably logged for audit purposes, ensuring that the process is both secure and transparent.” India’s government already operates several data exchanges, but it is unclear how much work remains to make DEPA a reality. Once DEPA is working, MeitY envisions model-makers will use it to do things like “unlock currently fragmented health data to power breakthroughs in AI-driven diagnostics, drug discovery, and public health management.” The optimism extends to financial services. India is home to literally thousands of banks, and MeitY thinks “DEPA can enable secure sharing of diverse financial data, potentially extending formal credit to 400 million underserved individuals and MSMEs and fueling next-generation fintech innovation.” India’s government has long believed that if financial services companies can lend to more people, it will boost economic development. “Similarly, in Education, DEPA can overcome data interoperability challenges to enable AI-powered personalized learning for millions and create portable skill credentials essential for a future-ready workforce of its 250 million students in a $29 billion EdTech sector,” the framework states. “The successful adoption of DEPA Training across these domains is the essential catalyst for realizing India’s vision of inclusive growth and responsible AI leadership on the global stage.” While the purpose of the framework is to build Indian AIs for Indians, the document also has half an eye on the nation’s international standing. “DEPA is India’s contribution to global science diplomacy, advancing the efforts of institutions such as the World Bank and the United Nations to shape a more inclusive and responsible global AI ecosystem,” the framework states. It also makes several mentions of digital public infrastructure (DPI), an idea pioneered by India that involves government funding creation of tools like the Unified Payments Interface payment systems and the Bharat Taxi zero-commission ride-sharing platform, to ensure Big Tech companies don’t dominate the local market. India also uses its DPI as a diplomatic tool, by giving it away to friendly nations. ®

Entities called “Training Data Consumers” (TDCs) access the data stored at the DEPs to train their models. DEPs will operate what MeitY calls “hardware-based Secure Data Environments” in which “data remains encrypted and isolated even during processing.” They also enforce rules set by TDPs that describe how TDCs can use data. MeitY’s DEPA framework [PDF] says this scheme means “Differential privacy techniques are systematically applied to prevent the model from learning or revealing individual specific information,” adding “All activities inside the secure data environments are immutably logged for audit purposes, ensuring that the process is both secure and transparent.” India’s government already operates several data exchanges, but it is unclear how much work remains to make DEPA a reality. Once DEPA is working, MeitY envisions model-makers will use it to do things like “unlock currently fragmented health data to power breakthroughs in AI-driven diagnostics, drug discovery, and public health management.” The optimism extends to financial services. India is home to literally thousands of banks, and MeitY thinks “DEPA can enable secure sharing of diverse financial data, potentially extending formal credit to 400 million underserved individuals and MSMEs and fueling next-generation fintech innovation.” India’s government has long believed that if financial services companies can lend to more people, it will boost economic development. “Similarly, in Education, DEPA can overcome data interoperability challenges to enable AI-powered personalized learning for millions and create portable skill credentials essential for a future-ready workforce of its 250 million students in a $29 billion EdTech sector,” the framework states. “The successful adoption of DEPA Training across these domains is the essential catalyst for realizing India’s vision of inclusive growth and responsible AI leadership on the global stage.” While the purpose of the framework is to build Indian AIs for Indians, the document also has half an eye on the nation’s international standing. “DEPA is India’s contribution to global science diplomacy, advancing the efforts of institutions such as the World Bank and the United Nations to shape a more inclusive and responsible global AI ecosystem,” the framework states. It also makes several mentions of digital public infrastructure (DPI), an idea pioneered by India that involves government funding creation of tools like the Unified Payments Interface payment systems and the Bharat Taxi zero-commission ride-sharing platform, to ensure Big Tech companies don’t dominate the local market. India also uses its DPI as a diplomatic tool, by giving it away to friendly nations. ®

items.title: Anthropic Adds a Claude Code Rule on Opus 5.5 That Blocks Recreations of Existing Games
items.summary: Anthropic has added a rule to Claude Code, its AI coding assistant, that stops the tool from recreating specific existing video games when it runs on the Opus 5.5 model. Anthropic confirmed the change through a post by Addy Osmani, a member of its technical staff, who said the company added two sentences to Claude Code's prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from rebuilding someone else's game. The rule reached Claude Code around October 27, according to X user Chasm, who first shared the change. Chasm reports that the instruction is delivered from Anthropic's servers under a flag named "tengu_heron_brook" and that users cannot switch it off. What the New Claude Code Rule Allows and Blocks The instruction tells Claude to keep building original games, games in an established genre, and games based on the user's own designs and assets. Recreating a specific existing game is off the table, and the rule says this applies "even if it is renamed or called original." In practice, the rule draws this line: allowed: original game concepts, genre games, and projects built from the developer's own designs and assets blocked: a copy of a specific existing game, including versions that carry a new name or are described as original Osmani says the reason is Anthropic's usage policy, which already prohibits using Claude to infringe intellectual property. The prompt change makes Claude Code enforce that policy directly when a request targets a particular game. Anthropic says it will continue to adjust the rule to strike the right balance. Osmani asked developers whose own projects are refused by Claude to send those cases to him directly. Why Anthropic Is Targeting AI Game Clones The change follows complaints about low-effort AI-generated games during Valve's Steam Next Fest in October. Players reported that their feeds filled up with clones of existing games, including copies of titles that had only just released their own demos. Some developers reacted by pulling public demos. The team behind Drunken Goddess Reflux, Alliance Arts and Who You, canceled its Steam demo plans in favor of private playtests. Valve responded that it would be "thinking about how to solve this problem." For developers who use Claude Code, the practical impact depends on the project. Original work and genre games should continue to work as before. Requests to reproduce a known game, or to rebuild one under a new title, now fail on Opus 5.5. Anthropic's previous Claude launch, the Claude Duet background agent , was limited to paying subscribers, while the game rule is applied server-side to Claude Code on Opus 5.5 with no user setting to disable it. Anthropic has not said whether a specific incident prompted the change, whether the rule will extend to other Claude models, or how it treats mods, decompilations, and recompilations of existing games. Thank you for being a Ghacks reader.

items.title: AI translation sounds convincing, but it can be riddled with hidden errors
items.summary: Jorg Greuel/Getty Images Generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools are more widespread than ever, and one of the functions they offer is fast, real-time translation. Some people are even questioning the need to ever learn another language , if near-instant translation is so widely available to all of us, often for free. However, those translations are far from perfect. While AI translations are very fluent, fluency doesn’t equal accuracy. Even proficient bilinguals can overlook errors hidden under the surface . Some of the mistakes in AI translation come from a lack of learning data, insufficient prompts, or even hallucations – confident presentation of false information, a hallmark of AI chatbots. Other errors reflect something more fundamental: the inherent complexity and flexibility of human language, and the linguistic or cultural differences between two languages. In my professional work reviewing real AI translations between English and Chinese, I have found some revealing examples of this problem. English and Chinese are two of the most used languages , with a large amount of data for AI to learn from; the issues could be more serious if you’re working on less common languages . For those using generative AI to translate, it’s important to keep these risks in mind. Where can AI translation go wrong? At word level Words can have multiple meanings and AI may not always choose the right one. In one translation I reviewed, an international student described Australian professors as laid back because they wore thongs to class. AI interpreted “thongs” as G-strings (underwear) rather than flip-flops (footwear). Tense can be problematic too. English verbs clearly indicate tense through forms such as “go”, “went” and “is going”. Chinese verbs don’t change in the same way. Instead, time is often conveyed through context or other words. When translating Chinese into English, AI can choose the wrong tense, changing whether something has happened, is happening or will happen. At sentence level A sentence can have different interpretations that are grammatically correct but different in meaning. For example, “You can see him in the store” can mean he is in the store – or you’re in the store when you see him. A human translator can often resolve such ambiguity by considering the context, but AI makes a decision by predicting the next possible words. And if a mistake is made, it can be difficult to spot later when the overall AI output sounds completely natural. Without careful checking against the original, the meaning can be changed without you noticing. At whole text level Accuracy involves more than getting individual words and sentences right. Information must also flow across a text, which is known as cohesion. And languages often achieve cohesion differently. For example, English frequently uses definite article “the” to refer back to something previously mentioned. “The” doesn’t exist in Chinese; cohesion is achieved by repeating the same word over and over throughout the text. AI can sometimes connect these references incorrectly, leaving readers confused about who or what is being discussed. Beyond communicating information Language doesn’t just communicate information. People also use it to establish relationships and connect with others. Different languages and cultures can build similar relationships in different ways, depending on cultural or ideological differences. For example, government communications in Australia often use “we” and “you” to build a closer relationship with the general public. By contrast, another language – such as Chinese – may prefer third person and more formal words for distance and authority. Translation is also about introducing new ideas to another language or reflecting evolving beliefs about existing expressions. For example, terms such as “ neurodiversity ” may not have widely established equivalents in another language. And when communities want to address stigma inherent to certain expressions, they might intentionally replace previously used words with new and emerging ones. For example, Chinese terminology referring to transgender people has evolved – more inclusive expressions are gaining recognition . AI may reproduce older or less appropriate terminology, particularly where newer expressions are underrepresented in its training data. A translation can therefore be linguistically understandable yet socially insensitive. So when can you trust AI translation? Just as AI is a black box, your AI translation is also a black box. No large language model can guarantee your AI translation always comes out perfectly. But overall, AI translation tends to be more reliable when: the topic is familiar and straightforward across two languages, not involving cultural difference or sensitive issues the original text is written in perfect grammar and clear sentence structure with no ambiguity the two languages are both among most widely used languages (such as English, Chinese, French or Spanish), which means more training data is available for AI to learn from you provide effective prompts: clearly define the context, the reader, the purpose, and the language features of the translation task. The translation provided by a chatbot will also be more accurate if it’s combined with neural machine translation technology – this is AI that’s dedicated to translation specifically and trained accordingly. It’s not a feature usually available on the common free AI platforms. However, even when all the boxes are ticked, accuracy can’t be guaranteed; errors can crop up, hallucinations can happen . You trust it at your own risk. Remember, generative AI doesn’t truly understand the complex and often ambiguous human experiences in a text. It may be good enough for understanding the general idea of a text, but its quality is never guaranteed without human input. items.summary_html:
Jorg Greuel/Getty Images

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools are more widespread than ever, and one of the functions they offer is fast, real-time translation. Some people are even questioning the need to ever learn another language, if near-instant translation is so widely available to all of us, often for free.

However, those translations are far from perfect. While AI translations are very fluent, fluency doesn’t equal accuracy. Even proficient bilinguals can overlook errors hidden under the surface.

Some of the mistakes in AI translation come from a lack of learning data, insufficient prompts, or even hallucations – confident presentation of false information, a hallmark of AI chatbots.

Other errors reflect something more fundamental: the inherent complexity and flexibility of human language, and the linguistic or cultural differences between two languages.

In my professional work reviewing real AI translations between English and Chinese, I have found some revealing examples of this problem. English and Chinese are two of the most used languages, with a large amount of data for AI to learn from; the issues could be more serious if you’re working on less common languages.

For those using generative AI to translate, it’s important to keep these risks in mind.

Where can AI translation go wrong?

At word level

Words can have multiple meanings and AI may not always choose the right one.

In one translation I reviewed, an international student described Australian professors as laid back because they wore thongs to class. AI interpreted “thongs” as G-strings (underwear) rather than flip-flops (footwear).

Tense can be problematic too. English verbs clearly indicate tense through forms such as “go”, “went” and “is going”. Chinese verbs don’t change in the same way. Instead, time is often conveyed through context or other words. When translating Chinese into English, AI can choose the wrong tense, changing whether something has happened, is happening or will happen.

At sentence level

A sentence can have different interpretations that are grammatically correct but different in meaning.

For example, “You can see him in the store” can mean he is in the store – or you’re in the store when you see him. A human translator can often resolve such ambiguity by considering the context, but AI makes a decision by predicting the next possible words.

And if a mistake is made, it can be difficult to spot later when the overall AI output sounds completely natural. Without careful checking against the original, the meaning can be changed without you noticing.

At whole text level

Accuracy involves more than getting individual words and sentences right. Information must also flow across a text, which is known as cohesion. And languages often achieve cohesion differently.

For example, English frequently uses definite article “the” to refer back to something previously mentioned. “The” doesn’t exist in Chinese; cohesion is achieved by repeating the same word over and over throughout the text.

AI can sometimes connect these references incorrectly, leaving readers confused about who or what is being discussed.

Beyond communicating information

Language doesn’t just communicate information. People also use it to establish relationships and connect with others.

Different languages and cultures can build similar relationships in different ways, depending on cultural or ideological differences. For example, government communications in Australia often use “we” and “you” to build a closer relationship with the general public. By contrast, another language – such as Chinese – may prefer third person and more formal words for distance and authority.

Translation is also about introducing new ideas to another language or reflecting evolving beliefs about existing expressions.

For example, terms such as “neurodiversity” may not have widely established equivalents in another language.

And when communities want to address stigma inherent to certain expressions, they might intentionally replace previously used words with new and emerging ones. For example, Chinese terminology referring to transgender people has evolved – more inclusive expressions are gaining recognition.

AI may reproduce older or less appropriate terminology, particularly where newer expressions are underrepresented in its training data. A translation can therefore be linguistically understandable yet socially insensitive.

So when can you trust AI translation?

Just as AI is a black box, your AI translation is also a black box. No large language model can guarantee your AI translation always comes out perfectly. But overall, AI translation tends to be more reliable when:

  • the topic is familiar and straightforward across two languages, not involving cultural difference or sensitive issues

  • the original text is written in perfect grammar and clear sentence structure with no ambiguity

  • the two languages are both among most widely used languages (such as English, Chinese, French or Spanish), which means more training data is available for AI to learn from

  • you provide effective prompts: clearly define the context, the reader, the purpose, and the language features of the translation task.

The translation provided by a chatbot will also be more accurate if it’s combined with neural machine translation technology – this is AI that’s dedicated to translation specifically and trained accordingly. It’s not a feature usually available on the common free AI platforms.

However, even when all the boxes are ticked, accuracy can’t be guaranteed; errors can crop up, hallucinations can happen. You trust it at your own risk.

Remember, generative AI doesn’t truly understand the complex and often ambiguous human experiences in a text. It may be good enough for understanding the general idea of a text, but its quality is never guaranteed without human input.
